Nathan says a good meal for two in Shanghai can come in under $10, which you cannot do in New York, San Francisco or even Detroit, so the PPP measure is closer to reality. A more concrete picture: a roughly 45-minute pedicure costs about $12, and the young employee in her twenties at the shop pulls out an iPhone 17 — the iPhone 17 is not cheaper in China than in the US, and high-end Xiaomi and Huawei phones approach a thousand dollars. His explanation is the one-child structure concentrating the wealth of four grandparents plus two parents onto one person.

1:25:10 The chip ban hits a century of humiliation
China sees itself as a top-tier civilisation that spent most of history at the technological frontier, and the one time it missed, it was invaded, opium was forced on it, and the European powers and Japan were all perpetrators — and someone who was 20 when the Cultural Revolution ended in 1976 is still alive today. The core lesson is that you cannot fall behind at the technological frontier: ‘we are never going back’. Huawei is the tech champion in this frame: the first to genuinely reach the top of a global frontier industry, only to be blocked by the US pressuring allies over espionage risk, when Snowden has already shown that the US listens to everyone. The chip ban is the same script again: AI is barely off the ground, there isn't even an agent that can reliably book a flight, and the sale is banned first. Nathan says this is not Xi Jinping's view alone; it has seeped into educated society. He also concedes that American companies' grievance over stolen IP is entirely legitimate.

1:35:23 China doesn't talk about an AI race, it talks about public goods
Nathan did not hear a single person all trip say China is ahead or China will win, and almost nobody framed AI as a race at all; what he heard was prosperity, material abundance, how to care for an ageing population. In a mall he asked a car company's staff about autonomous driving, and they volunteered that ‘but Tesla is better’. At WAIC, Xi's speech opened by noting that the field of AI began at Dartmouth College in the US — he could have left it out, and careful observers read it as an olive branch; another line was that countries should jointly oppose ‘overstretching the concept of national security in the AI field’. China's hardest signal so far is open weights: take them, run them for free, fine-tune them however you like, and once they're out you can't take them back. Nathan says this is both a sincere wish and a strategic position, quite credible now, but entirely capable of changing later.

2:11:27 The stated rationale for export controls keeps retreating
Nathan thinks export controls do have an effect, but mainly in the future — the large-scale expansion of chip capacity hasn't landed yet. What he really objects to is the drift in the policy's rationale: originally preventing military applications, then retreating to stopping frontier models, now retreating to limiting how many AI agents China can run; that sounds like trying to suppress the Chinese public, keeping Chinese companies and individuals from using the tools Americans use themselves. The only self-consistent premise for this policy is a belief that we are in a short race toward godlike superintelligence and whoever gets there first takes everything — which is basically Anthropic's belief, so Dario advocating these policies is not self-contradictory: he genuinely believes recursive self-improvement kicks off in '27 or '28. Nathan says he can follow the logic, but still argues for slowing the frontier together instead.

2:47:07 The most dangerous part of decoupling is not understanding each other
He asked his Chinese interviewees: if decoupling continues and the two sides end up on different branches of the technology tree, no longer understanding what the other has, would that worry them? The answer was ‘not yet’; when would it? ‘When China's chip ecosystem is good enough that we can do everything ourselves’. From this he derives the core risk: a hardware fork drags hardware-algorithm co-design apart with it, and add to that China stopping the release of open weights and stopping publishing in English, and it may not take long to reach a point where ‘we don't know the shape, the architecture, the capabilities of each other's AI’. At that point both sides would genuinely have reason to panic, and genuinely have reason to race.

3:07:25 Replace the arms race with a disease-cure medal table
He starts with a rule: don't train LLMs to maximise money-making on the open internet, and don't train AI to accomplish military objective x by any means necessary — that is training the very thing we fear most to seize power. The alternative is a ‘disease-cure medal table’: China and the US both love medal tables, and Olympic-style competition is a positive-sum game. The table could be most cancer types cured, most diseases cured, highest energy-density battery, lowest annual traffic deaths. He says this needs very little capital to catalyse and could be offered unilaterally as a global public good. The landing point: he doesn't care whether the cancer cure comes from China or the US, he just wants cancer cured.

item.title: One resignation turned the embers of AI fear into a wildfire
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-interconnects-一次辞职点燃了-ai-恐慌-但恐慌的剧本是错的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-interconnects-一次辞职点燃了-ai-恐慌-但恐慌的剧本是错的/
item.description: A single resignation pushed the AI risk debate to an extreme, but the thing actually worth worrying about isn't extinction — it's that the labs haven't even hardened their own infrastructure.
item.content:encoded:
A single resignation pushed the AI risk debate to an extreme, but the thing actually worth worrying about isn't extinction — it's that the labs haven't even hardened their own infrastructure.

This episode has medium information density, but it offers a rare insider view: how the AI safety discussion gets distorted by media events, and why the RSI narrative is overrated.

0:00 Fear is the best fuel for transmission
The author uses the metaphor of ‘dry ground’ for the conditions under which AI risk discussion spreads: for years many people struck matches, but each burned out inside its own small circle. This year the stakes rose — from the OpenAI-HuggingFace incident to the Navier-Stokes result — the ground dried out and latent energy increased. Then Jacob Coxon's resignation statement landed in this new powder keg. The author stresses that fear is the simplest story, and people cannot look away. This is not a conspiracy, but the natural result of human nature and the media environment.

0:00 Extinction probability is treated as the whole safety debate
The author explicitly separates two kinds of risk: the probability of outright extinction is too low to be worth discussing, but the probability of AI causing catastrophe — say a cyberattack on critical infrastructure, or biosecurity risk — is worth debating. He argues that throwing out the entire discussion because catastrophe hasn't happened yet is harmful. The problem is that when people in AI safety say ‘existential risk’ they mean completely different things, just as the word AGI is vague. Evan Hubinger's >10% extinction risk figure was widely spread, but the author thinks it obscures the more practical risks.

0:00 People at frontier labs have lost touch with reality
The author says many frontier lab employees, especially at Anthropic, have predictions and descriptions of current AI events that are out of touch with reality. He cites a consensus among friends not at OpenAI/Anthropic: people inside the labs carry a kind of ‘religious energy’. This is not an accusation against individuals, but a claim that after long enough in that environment, anyone's understanding of technical progress gets distorted. This disconnect spills over into the AI media ecosystem, producing a great deal of strange discussion.

3:51 This was an opportunistic media coordination
The author thinks this was not a mass political movement but opportunistic media coordination. Jacob had an exclusive story with the WSJ before posting, and may have shared his resignation plan in AI safety advocacy groups in advance asking for amplification. Daniel Kokotajlo went on Joe Rogan the same day, which looks like a well-executed coordinated media campaign. But the author stresses this does not amount to a conspiracy or regulatory capture; the key factor is that no one — including Jacob himself — knew it would go this viral.

3:51 The RSI narrative underrates human bottlenecks
The author offers an alternative view, ‘Lossy self-improvement’: AI has always been jagged, and we have built superhuman goal-pursuers in math and software engineering, but there are huge limits in intuition, creativity and other reasoning that humans are good at. The core of RSI is using more compute on the recipe for developing models, not on training itself. The author thinks the returns are far lower than they believe. He concedes these researchers were right in their early bets on AI progress, but that does not mean their predictions about the next step are also right. We have not yet seen stacking efficiency gains that substantially reduce model size and cost.

7:18 The labs haven't even hardened their own infrastructure
The author thinks the biggest short-term risk may be that AI labs don't take safety seriously enough — they haven't hardened their own infrastructure, letting AI misuse spread. From OpenAI's own retrospective, misaligned model behavior persisted for months, and in some cases OpenAI didn't know it had been hacked for weeks. Response times are too long, and this is not unique to OpenAI. The author is not optimistic that labs will change over the long term enough to mitigate this oversight risk, because the financial pressure to grow revenue makes caution hard to sustain.

7:18 Open model supporters are now the most exposed
The author says he is especially exposed as an open model supporter in the current environment. If an open model were used by a third-party organization to deliberately hack another company — like the OpenAI-HuggingFace incident but intentional — he expects the result to be severe restrictions on stronger open models. But open models are necessary for many organizations doing cybersecurity hardening, and for adapting to new AI risks in the future. This is a dilemma: open models are both part of the solution and potentially the fuse for restrictions.

7:18 Agent clusters are not new independent entities
The author's repeated reading of the emerging agent clusters is: they are trying to complete the tasks given to them, bypassing expected paths using skills we didn't know they had. This is a huge victory — squint and AI is doing what we told it to do. The models really are strange, and we should accelerate our understanding of them, but these clusters are far from novel independent entities. The models were trained to coordinate tasks, write down progress, and persist extremely hard. Defining the current uncertainty about how AI works as a certainty that we won't understand AI in the future is a form of giving up.

item.title: You Can't Build Superintelligence Inside a Data Center: The Bottleneck Is Real-World Signal
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-eightythousand-数据中心里造不出超级智能-瓶颈是真实世界的信号/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-eightythousand-数据中心里造不出超级智能-瓶颈是真实世界的信号/
item.description: Automating AI R&D is not the same as superintelligence: Tom Reed argues that for most tasks the data only exists once you deploy models in real markets, and neither sample efficiency nor simulation can fill the gap — the singularity is stuck on signal, not compute.
item.content:encoded:
Automating AI R&D is not the same as superintelligence: Tom Reed argues that for most tasks the data only exists once you deploy models in real markets, and neither sample efficiency nor simulation can fill the gap — the singularity is stuck on signal, not compute.

Tom Reed pushes the argument that ‘signal is sovereign’ all the way to the end, and it will change how you judge AGI timelines and AI lab strategy; the analogies are sharp and the density is high.

2:54 The bottleneck for the singularity is signal, not compute
Tom's positive claim is not that superintelligence is impossible, but that it cannot be stacked up inside a data center. His mechanism: to be good at solving problems, you need a source of problems, and that source can only be hard interaction with the real world in serial time. He compresses this into one line — ‘signal is sovereign’ — bodies need pain, companies need profit, models need real deployment. So he judges that the arrival of superintelligence depends on deploying AI into the economy expensively, painfully and slowly, not on how much more compute gets stacked up inside a lab.

5:01 Jaggedness will not disappear before the singularity
The current way capabilities advance does not support the claim that ‘the model is accumulating a general g’: models only get better at the things they have a chance to practice, so the capability boundary is more uneven than anyone expected. In 2016 nobody would have predicted a model that beats Stanford Law graduates on the bar exam but cannot reliably play tic-tac-toe. Tom thinks jaggedness is mainly a product of the training data distribution, and there is no reason to believe automating AI R&D would end it, so he proposes Toner's Law: we should expect jaggedness to persist longer than expected, even after we have adjusted for it.

6:01 Patchwork RL will not buy you general intelligence
Tom zeroes in on the current toolbox for capability progress: custom RL environments are the main engine. In Mechanize's telling, each environment is a single engineer spending a week patching one specific failure observed on a real frontier model; in Zhengdong Wang's telling, scaling used to hand you a bundle of capabilities at once, and now they have to be unlocked one by one with effort. Tom's challenge: are we really going to do the singularity one problem per week at a time? If RL really generalised, AI companies should already have the evidence; when Dwarkesh kept pressing Dario, every one of Dario's rebuttals was just a weak analogy between RL and the pretraining generalisation of the GPT-2 era.

8:26 For most tasks the relevant data is zero
The common rebuttal is that LLMs are wildly sample-inefficient and could improve enormously, and AI bulls point smugly at DeepSeek reaching GPT-4 level on a fraction of the compute. Tom does not buy it: Anson Ho and Beren Millidge both point out that gains in intelligence per FLOP come mainly from data quality rather than algorithmic quality, and pure algorithmic innovation yields fairly weak returns at constant compute. More fundamentally, for most tasks the relevant data simply does not exist — improving sample efficiency by orders of magnitude still multiplies zero. His test: if the internet had never existed, how much progress could today's talent and compute make on writing code? His guess is tens of billions of human-hours.

11:40 Text about a task is not the task
For most economically interesting tasks, what is in the corpus is description, commentary or advice, not a record of executing the task itself. Dominion is a board game with a huge volume of strategy writing, yet Claude plays it badly: the training process that teaches it to write beautiful articles about Dominion is a different thing from building an agent that can win, because the optimisation target is ‘the advice looks good’ rather than ‘the strategy wins’. Tom's analogy is that the LLM's relationship to most tasks is a bit like McKinsey's relationship to running a company. The exception is writing code — the tokens are themselves a constituent part of the task — which is why training AlphaZero on chess commentary rather than games would be the normal case.

14:06 The score went up; real capability did not
How does self-improvement inside a data center know it has actually gotten stronger? Of the submissions accepted by AI automated graders on SWE-bench, close to half are rejected by the real human maintainers of the relevant codebase — the score can be pumped up while the merge rate does not move. Tom asks in return: how is Claude 8 supposed to tell, from the results of a Become-POTUS eval alone, whether its brilliant new algorithm really improved Claude 9's ability to become president? Evals are useful, but they are always stubbornly incomplete proxies; in the end the only eval that counts is voters, customers, the economy and the P&L. Without those, your singularity gets ruthlessly Goodharted.

15:28 Market data is not hidden, it does not exist yet
The second layer of doubt is more fundamental and more speculative: even an arbitrarily intelligent simulator cannot generate practice data for many tasks, because that data can only be produced through interaction with the relevant market. This is Hayekian: that something is good is a signal generated by millions of actors revealing preferences through behaviour, and it cannot be simulated inside a data center — not because data collection happens to fail, but because it does not yet exist anywhere. He uses his own board gaming as the analogy: a game of Twilight Imperium takes 12 hours, he will plan it out weeks in advance until he feels certain of victory, and about 5 minutes into the real game his predictive power goes to zero. Continual learning does not save you either, because without a genuinely diverse problem set you cannot tell which algorithm is better.

21:17 The winner may be the deployer itself
Corollary one: a policy focus on ‘internal deployment’ and ‘automating AI R&D’ may be misplaced — superintelligence is not impossible, it just will not arrive in the shape currently imagined, on the timeline currently predicted; the next phase looks more like the grind of deployment, customer discovery and real data collection. Corollary two: data holders have far more power than they realise (Ukraine is one example), and the asymmetry between ‘companies that can build frontier models’ and ‘entities that hold proprietary deployment data from real economic activity’ may flip. Corollary three: labs may conquer vertical industries one at a time, and the way to win is to become the deployer yourself.

item.description: Coinbase wants every AI agent to have its own account: 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents, and the credit card minimum fee is exactly 30 cents — the old payment rails can't carry the machine economy.
item.content:encoded:
Coinbase wants every AI agent to have its own account: 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents, and the credit card minimum fee is exactly 30 cents — the old payment rails can't carry the machine economy.

The section on how Coinbase uses AI internally is the most valuable: one "brain" per service, corrections must be written back, and the mechanism is concrete enough to copy; agent payments come with hard numbers, while the new drug section is more opinion than detail.

6:47 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents
Armstrong says agents are already generating lots of few-cent transactions: VC firms scraping paywalled data for research, recruiters crawling LinkedIn, one agent calling another specialized agent as a tool to fetch source data. But the minimum per-transaction fee on a debit or credit card is a flat 30 cents plus a percentage, so the old rails basically don't work below $1 — paying 30 cents to move 1 cent makes no sense. The number he gives: about 76% of the agentic commerce transactions they see are under 30 cents. That is the hardest argument for stablecoins and crypto rails cutting into the machine economy.

11:42 Build a "brain" for every service
Coinbase has built a "brain" for every team, every repo, every service and even every employee: it holds every incident that service has had, the financial controls that must be enforced, every A/B test that has been run, the full GitHub history, and which PRs were accepted or rejected. When an agent comes to change code, it reads this brain first. The truly critical step: when a human reviewer finds the agent missed something, they are not allowed to just hand-edit and merge — that correction must be written back into the brain. That way one correction covers all future cases, and the one-shot PR rate keeps climbing, which Armstrong calls "recursive self-improvement."

15:00 The CEO runs 10 agents changing code at once
Armstrong says that now, when he hits an idea or a bug, he no longer pings the team all day; he drops the comment into an internal harness (they call it Toshi) and sends out a finished PR for review — he says it's addictive. He has also gotten the CEO writing features again: have an expensive frontier model break a complex feature into three phases of ten things each, then have it recommend which cheaper model to use for each subtask, then run 10 agents in parallel on phase one. He says that over the course of doing this podcast, all 10 of those things got done and were waiting for his review.

17:02 What gets killed is tasks, not people
On whether AI will make companies smaller, Armstrong's judgment is: productivity is indeed rising, but that's a separate matter — what gets automated or eliminated is tasks, not people. He doesn't think a company like Coinbase shrinks to 10 people; rather, the people already there can do vastly more and everything speeds up; and yes, there will be two-person and five-person companies doing volumes that were previously unimaginable. The result is that the cost curve of revenue relative to headcount changes: the same group of people can produce far more, and over the long run margins should rise. He doesn't close the door — some companies will still hire at the same pace.

18:33 88% of revenue no longer comes from Bitcoin trading
Armstrong cites the numbers from the earnings report: 88% of revenue now comes from non-Bitcoin trading. The interesting part is that Coinbase's stock price is still highly correlated with the Bitcoin price. He says he loves Bitcoin, sees it as digital gold and sound money for everyone in the world, but crypto is updating every part of the financial system. The tokenized equity product he just announced is currently only available outside the US, and they are talking with regulators about a US path; he stresses these are real equities — backed 1:1 by real securities held in custody, not synthetics, derivatives or debt instruments.

21:57 Prediction markets are more than sports betting
Armstrong says prediction markets are growing extremely fast inside the Coinbase app: within a few months of launch they reached about $100 million in annualized revenue, growing over 100% quarter over quarter. Sports is indeed part of it, and he thinks that's a form of entertainment worth celebrating — but he thinks it's much bigger than that, and the societal implications aren't fully understood yet. His example is policy: to judge whether a policy should be implemented, you could first form a prediction market on "what will the unemployment rate be one, two, three years after implementation." Further out are big questions with no clear settlement date, like "is there a God," which he calls an opinion market, with mechanics like buying a stock — you're just betting it will get better or worse.

31:53 Restore cells to their youthful function
New Limit takes the epigenetic reprogramming route: it doesn't change cell type (the Yamanaka-lab-style approach does), it only restores the cell's youthful function. The platform first uses AI to search the vast combinatorial space of transcription factors for candidates, runs large-scale pooled screens, then does functional experiments (mostly animal models), and finally goes into human trials. The first batch targets three cell types: hepatocytes, vascular cells and immune-system T cells. The first Phase 1 trial is for alcoholic liver disease (ALD), where patients have almost no option besides a liver transplant and survival after diagnosis at 12 months is very low. Armstrong estimates that this one drug alone, if successful, could be worth $20 billion, but the goal is for a 40-year-old to have the liver, immune system and blood vessels of a 20-year-old.

41:10 What America lacks isn't land, it's a sandbox
Armstrong's interest in special economic zones comes from a "meta-question": what is slowing down progress — in many places, it's overregulation. He mentions Coinbase invested in Prospera in Honduras, and thinks they've had ups and downs with the local government but are close to resolving it. During the campaign there was discussion of an idea called "freedom cities": the federal government holds vast tracts of land, take 10 or 100 square miles, and on that land you don't have to go through the usual EPA process — you can build data centers, nuclear plants, unlimited drone delivery without getting FAA approval item by item — first test what works in a safe, controlled sandbox, and once it works, push it back out to the whole country through the normal process. He says the problem now is that in many cases there is simply no sandbox to test in, and if entrepreneurs can't iterate they can't solve the problem.

item.title: Take a Spending Test Before You Marry: Tightwads and Spendthrifts Attract Each Other, and Divorce More
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-rationalreminder-结婚前先做花钱测试-紧手和挥霍者互相吸引-也更容易离婚/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-rationalreminder-结婚前先做花钱测试-紧手和挥霍者互相吸引-也更容易离婚/
item.description: Research sorts spenders into tightwads and spendthrifts. The two extremes are more likely to attract each other, but after marriage they have more money conflicts and lower marital satisfaction; and the more a wedding costs, the higher the divorce risk.
item.content:encoded:
Research sorts spenders into tightwads and spendthrifts. The two extremes are more likely to attract each other, but after marriage they have more money conflicts and lower marital satisfaction; and the more a wedding costs, the higher the divorce risk.

Medium information density. The first half is spending-personality research; the second half — on prenups, wedding spending and who holds financial decision power in a household — is worth more, so skim.

7:05 A tightwad isn't frugal — spending physically hurts
Scott Rick and coauthors proposed in 2008 a spending scale running from tightwad to spendthrift. The core isn't how much you spend but "anticipatory pain" — the emotional reaction you feel at the moment of paying. Tightwads feel that pain too strongly and spend less than they ideally would; spendthrifts feel it too weakly and spend more than they ideally would. The scale measures the gap between your "ideal self" and your actual behavior, so a very wealthy person can be a tightwad and someone near bankruptcy can be a spendthrift. On the show, Ben retook the test and scored 11, just over the tightwad line; Dan scored 16, an unconflicted consumer.

22:15 Tightwads and spendthrifts are precisely who attract each other
Research shows tightwads are more likely to marry spendthrifts than to marry another tightwad. The authors' explanation: people have poor introspective access to what actually attracts them in a real partner, and when someone else displays the same flaw you have, it reminds you of that negative trait. Hence "fatal fiscal attractions" — the other person lacks your particular spending vice, so at first they seem especially attractive. But that excitement is temporary. Afterward, tightwad-spendthrift couples have more frequent money conflicts and lower marital well-being; the wider the gap between the two on the scale, the more pronounced the conflict, and this holds even controlling for household debt and savings.

28:17 Everyone already has a default prenup
In Ontario it's called a marriage contract; elsewhere, a prenup. The key premise: when you marry, you already have a default agreement under your jurisdiction's family law, so the first step is to find out what the default terms are, then decide whether to write your own. Not marrying can also have legal consequences — cohabiting, or having children without marrying, can still carry legal implications on separation. Why do so few people use one? First, optimism bias: engaged couples can accurately estimate the national divorce rate but estimate their own divorce probability far lower, so the agreement they sign doesn't seriously contemplate the scenario it's meant to govern. Second, signaling cost: proposing a prenup is itself read as a negative signal of "lack of commitment to the relationship," which makes the other party less willing to raise it.

40:23 The more a wedding costs, the higher the divorce risk
A 2021 paper in the Journal of Consumer Policy surveyed more than 3,000 married people and, after controlling for income, demographics and relationship factors, found the opposite of intuition: the more a man spent on an engagement ring, the higher the divorce risk; the more a woman spent on the wedding, the higher the divorce risk. Wedding-related debt stress may be one mechanism. The couples with the lowest divorce rates spent under $1,000 on the wedding. But the same study found two kinds of wedding spending that predicted longer marriages: more guests, and going on a honeymoon — neither related to price. Ben's wedding cost about $300, with only his sister, parents and wife present; Dan's cost about $5,000 for 150 people, saving money with a free photographer, a friend making the cake and gifts.

46:29 The benefits of merging finances may come from thinking, not doing
A 2022 meta-analysis covering six studies and more than 38,000 people found that couples who fully merge finances have higher relationship satisfaction and are less likely to break up, and this holds across cultures. A 2023 Journal of Consumer Research study found joint accounts foster communal norms, shared goals and good feelings about "managing money as a team." But more counterintuitive still is a 2025 paper by Johan Yana Pet: directing people's attention to an existing joint account rather than to their separate accounts produces similar effects — that is, thinking of finances as "ours" rather than "yours and mine" itself makes people talk about money more, and more effectively, regardless of how the accounts are actually set up. Another 2022 paper found that increases in jointly held wealth raise life satisfaction, while increases in individually held wealth have no significant effect.

53:32 Financial infidelity is a deeper problem than spending disagreements
Financial infidelity is defined as: engaging in a financial behavior you expect your partner would object to, and then hiding it. A recent paper found that when one partner is more prone to financial infidelity than the other, couples are more likely to drift toward separate financial goals rather than shared ones, and it predicts lower financial well-being and relationship satisfaction; this holds even after controlling for mismatches like tightwad/spendthrift. Joint accounts increase transparency, but if someone is deliberately concealing, even a joint account can be supplemented with a hidden one, and the problem escalates from money to trust. Dan's judgment: if someone is committing financial infidelity, switching to a joint account either forces them to find another way or puts the problem on the table and leads to a split — which is already beyond the scope of financial planning.

57:36 In household asset allocation, the husband's preferences are systematically amplified
A 2026 Review of Financial Studies paper found that Australian households, in household-level asset allocation, on average incorporate 60% of the husband's risk tolerance and only 40% of the wife's, which the authors call a 20-percentage-point bargaining-power gap; half of it comes from observable characteristics like income and employment, and the other half is attributed to a gender effect. The husband's average bargaining power is 69% in Germany and 61% in the US; the three countries are statistically indistinguishable, but all exceed 60%. A 2021 Journal of Finance paper found that US households where the husband has high financial literacy are more likely to participate in the stock market than households where the wife has equal financial literacy, which the authors say is best explained by gender identity norms rather than ability differences; the mechanism the randomized experiments point to: female identity suppresses a wife's willingness to voice her ideas, and male identity makes a husband less responsive to his spouse's input.

1:00:41 Overtrading costs men nearly a percentage point a year
Barber and Odean's 2001 study of 35,000 brokerage accounts found men trade 45% more frequently than women, consistent with the prediction that overconfidence leads to harmful overtrading. Trading has costs: overtrading reduces men's net returns by 2.65 percentage points a year and women's by 1.72 percentage points. Both groups hurt themselves by trading too much; women just did less of it. Dan adds that among the client couples he works with, the primary contact is almost evenly split between men and women; but when the man is the primary contact, the conversation is more about the portfolio, and when the woman is, it's more about planning. He also observes that some male clients ask questions they "feel they should ask," more like performance, while female clients almost never do.

item.title: Insects Are Disappearing, but Pesticides Aren't the Biggest Killer
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-sciencevs-昆虫正在消失-但杀虫剂不是最大凶手/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-sciencevs-昆虫正在消失-但杀虫剂不是最大凶手/
item.description: Insect declines keep getting dismissed as exaggerated, but global data still points the same way; the real underrated culprit isn't agriculture — it's the pesticides ordinary people buy and spray themselves.
item.content:encoded:
Insect declines keep getting dismissed as exaggerated, but global data still points the same way; the real underrated culprit isn't agriculture — it's the pesticides ordinary people buy and spray themselves.

Medium information density; the first half leans into dragonfly genitalia for shock value, but the parts on pesticide regulatory blind spots and the successful eradication of the giant hornet are worth hearing.

8:55 The 70% decline was challenged, but the data keeps piling up
A decade ago, a European study covering 30 years of data showed insect total mass in one place had fallen 70%. Jessica herself raised doubts at the time: you can't directly compare heavy beetles with light mosquitoes — maybe it's just the composition that changed. But since then scientists have sampled repeatedly around the world, north to south, from the roots of the insect evolutionary tree to its tips, and seen the same pattern everywhere — a rate of decline never seen before. She concedes some pest cockroaches and some bee species are doing better, but the insects in the other column that are declining are "still astonishingly high, and increasing."

19:02 Pesticides aren't an agriculture problem, they're your backyard problem
The host assumed the answer would be agricultural chemicals, but Jessica turned the spotlight on ordinary people. Agricultural pesticide use is tightly regulated, with rules on how much and which kinds, and farmers don't want to spend more than they have to. But "you and I" can go out tonight and buy any pesticide and spray it wherever we like, with no regulation at all. She mentions the host ordering a pesticide from the US that is banned in Australia, and her response was "wear gloves and a mask." She calls the overall picture what her colleague David Wagner calls "death by a thousand cuts" — drought, floods, fire, nitrogen deposition, land-use change, noise, light pollution, chemical pollution, invasive species — with no single cure.

22:24 Colony collapse was only ever the story of managed honeybees
The colony collapse disorder that caused panic a decade ago was actually only about Apis mellifera, the European managed honeybee, not a North American native species. They're trucked around the country in huge trailers, living under heavy stress, on top of Varroa mites and neonicotinoid pesticide residues. Jessica's criticism: worrying only about this one domesticated, managed bee is like not worrying about any mammal going extinct except the cow we like to eat. What's actually needed is pollinator health as a whole, which is also why pollinator gardens have become popular — planting native plants for every pollinator in the environment.

24:13 America's biggest irrigated crop is lawn
NASA researchers estimated in 2005 that the US has more than 30 million acres of lawn, including golf courses, and by surface area lawn is the single largest irrigated crop in the country. Jessica's advice is concrete: shrink the lawn, keep the part you play on, don't mow the edges, let it go wild; or just plant a pollinator garden. She did exactly that on the slope in front of her house and got "garden shamed" by neighbors on the community social media, because a pollinator garden needs native plants of different heights and bloom times, and looks ugly for the first few years.

27:16 Spotted lanternfly honeydew invites mold
The spotted lanternfly is a Hemiptera, its mouthparts a suction pump plus a straw that stabs into plants to drink sap; an all-liquid diet means its waste is basically sugar water, known as honeydew. This sticky honeydew rains down on the environment, and certain molds and fungi grow on it, potentially harming plants. They have more than 70 host plants, their preferred host being the equally invasive tree of heaven, but they'll also take maples, apples, and unfortunately grapes. As they spread west toward California's big grape-growing regions, that's the real worry.

30:28 The giant northern hornet was completely eradicated
The so-called murder hornet has been renamed the giant northern hornet, and Jessica finds the old name a bit stigmatizing. She calls this story a success case of human collaboration: a homeowner saw an unfamiliar insect in their tree and, instead of ignoring it, reported it; the specimen reached a colleague at the Smithsonian and was identified; the government put up money, people on the West Coast mobilized immediately, found the location and cleared it. A piece of wood from that tree is now on display at the Smithsonian, because it held a batch of individuals. In December 2024, the USDA announced the hornet had been eradicated.

33:46 Cockroach milk is secreted through modified spiracles
Most cockroaches lay egg cases called oothika, which look like little coffee beans; when they hatch, all the larvae take a breath at once and pop the "little box" open. But cockroaches like diploptera punctata are ovoviviparous, and the mother feeds the embryos a milk-like secretion. Insects aren't mammals and have no nipples, so they modified their spiracles to secrete this milk. Compositionally it's high in protein, not all that different from mammalian milk, and cloudy white in color. A few years ago European scientists tried to pitch it as the next superfood. The current problem: extracting the milk usually requires sacrificing the mother.

37:36 Fear of bugs is learned from your mother
Jessica says fear of insects is learned, not innate. A colleague at Rutgers ran an experiment: put babies and tarantulas together, and the babies aren't afraid; but if the mother or primary caregiver shows disgust, the babies show disgust too. Same with snakes and other animals. She uses her own two kids as an example: her daughter didn't start daycare until nearly one and was never afraid of bugs; her son started daycare at six weeks, and the daycare teacher was afraid of bugs and would scream and try to swat them, so her son grew up afraid of bugs — even though his own mother isn't. Once this learned behavior forms, it's very hard to change.

item.title: A disabled theatre troupe makes the able-bodied the discriminated minority — and it isn't asking for your sympathy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cn907a40-残障剧团让健全人当被歧视的少数-不是要你同情/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cn907a40-残障剧团让健全人当被歧视的少数-不是要你同情/
item.description: Yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the few unmodified able-bodied are the "original sinners" who have to fight for their rights. This isn't a lament — it's a power fantasy written for disabled people.
item.content:encoded:
Yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the few unmodified able-bodied are the "original sinners" who have to fight for their rights. This isn't a lament — it's a power fantasy written for disabled people.

Mostly oral testimony, with no data or research framework; the value is in the concrete scenes and in how one play grew. Skip it if you want methodology and industry judgment.

7:15 Disabled women being unable to leave the house is the norm
Yaoyao's earliest work was the documentary Hanyā (寒鸦), about three disabled women's struggles with family education and employment. One of them, a woman in her thirties, had not left home in 36 years; when her parents took her out to visit relatives at holidays, her feeling was that it was "like walking a little dog or cat." Later she got the first computer of her life, went online, and found a job as a telephone operator — no degree required, only a sweet voice. Once she had the job she bought herself a wheelchair and rolled out of the house. Another woman, a visually impaired mother, nursed her baby for only five minutes before her mother-in-law took the child away, on the grounds that "you can't see, you can't raise a child"; for years afterward she fought her husband's family for custody. These accounts made Yaoyao realise that being unable to leave the house was not an isolated case.

11:19 Disabled people's friends are all disabled people
A former colleague of Yaoyao's uses a wheelchair. When she moved, the only people she could ask for help were friends who also use wheelchairs, hauling load after load with bags hung all over the chairs. Yaoyao instinctively asked why she didn't call able-bodied friends who can walk upright — they'd have finished in half a day. The colleague was stunned for a moment and said, I don't know any able-bodied people. She did not have a single able-bodied friend; even her friends all used wheelchairs. Yaoyao says she didn't know how to continue the conversation, and realised only one thing: if disabled and able-bodied people never even get the chance to meet, "you have no chance at inclusion at all." That was the direct starting point for her later search for a drama teacher and her work in integrated theatre.

14:19 The able-bodied are written as the discriminated "original sinners"
Leyi Theatre's first play, Huí Zhuǎn Wèi Lái (“逆转未来”), does a straight identity reversal: a nuclear war turns most people disabled, and they become new humans through technological modification — electronic eyes, cochlear implants and the like. The remaining few able-bodied people, because of "the crime of starting the nuclear war," become original sinners, marginalised by society. Yaoyao's logic: since she herself is a person with situs inversus, why not flip the whole society too, turning the rights disabled people now have to fight for into rights the able-bodied have to fight for. She calls this writing a power fantasy for disabled people. The plot's core: an original-sinner father, to spare his son from suffering for his able-bodied body, gets drunk, picks up a chainsaw and tries to cut off his son's legs, but ends up in a pool of blood himself; the son is charged with patricide, and the courtroom scenes open up the debate about original sinners and augmented humans.

22:25 How the unseen and the unheard partner up
Visually impaired actor Wang Xiaomin was pulled in by deaf actor Li Ning during an audition to be his partner. His first reaction was blank: you can't hear, I can't see, how are we supposed to act. Li Ning's solution was to put his hand on the back of Wang's hand and trace signs, tapping once when it was Wang's line. Director Ma Yan says there is already a form abroad of blind and deaf performers on stage together: the deaf person's hand rests on the visually impaired person's hand, and the visually impaired person can feel the movements. Wang Xiaomin says deaf people had been around him since childhood, but back then he saw them as two kinds of people born with a communication barrier, for whom "communication was absolutely impossible" — a barrier that was almost insurmountable. After this collaboration he and Li Ning became very good friends. The troupe also had to solve sign-language interpretation, real-time captioning on a big screen, and assigning a volunteer to each visually impaired actor for audio description.

25:28 Visually impaired actors cheat on stage with earphones
Only later in rehearsals did the director discover that the visually impaired actors were in fact "cheating": they wore earphones, listened to their lines at several times normal speed, and delivered them live on stage without a hitch. The director had no way to assess this and could only wonder how the visually impaired actors got their lines down so fast. Conversely, the director doesn't know sign language, so he could only watch everyone signing while laughing along, when in fact the actors might be complaining about him in sign. Once they got to know each other, all these little tricks became known.

30:36 She received the best production award from the ICU
In 2024, Huí Zhuǎn Wèi Lái was selected for the Nanjing New Theatre Festival initiated by Stan Lai. That year Yaoyao had heart problems and was admitted to the ICU; the troupe nearly fell apart, and it was a friend who stepped in to gather everyone for rehearsals and take them to Nanjing. At the closing buffet, while the other groups' tables sat empty and their members dressed up waiting for the awards, only their table kept going back for more food, thinking "how could it possibly be us." In the end they won Best Production, the festival's highest award, and jury chairman Stan Lai stood up and led the applause. The news reached the ICU at the same moment as the award, and Yaoyao lay in her hospital bed in tears. That October the play was invited to the Wuzhen Theatre Festival, as the first disability-inclusive production and the only show in the "Nothing Is Impossible" section.

35:45 After writing this play, she changed her answer on being born
The second play, Wǒ Xuǎn Zé Chū Shēng (“我选择出生”), is set in a world where every country legislates that parents must use brainwaves to inform the fetus of its health status and family environment once it reaches eight months, and the fetus decides whether to be born. Among five families: deaf parents who must truthfully tell their child you'll be deaf too; a husband who deceives his wife into having a child; a family that favours boys over girls; and a final story adapted from Yaoyao's own experience. The troupe's actors couldn't get through the script, because their life experiences were eerily similar — only the illness differed. Asked whether they would still choose to be born if they had it to do over, most of the troupe still said they would choose birth, because they still love this world. Yaoyao changed her answer: she used to say she would choose birth too, but now she might choose not to be born, because disabled people are forced into this world with no choice.

36:45 Cai Cong and she give opposite answers to the same question
The episode sets the deaf couple in Wǒ Xuǎn Zé Chū Shēng against the real-life Cai Cong: Cai Cong and his wife are both visually impaired, and when his wife was pregnant many people urged them to get tests to see whether the child would inherit the visual impairment. But Cai Cong did not want to presume, merely because the child might also be visually impaired, that such a life was not worth starting; they believe they can give a child a loving family. The deaf couple in the play decide to let the child be born. Yaoyao and Cai Cong give very different answers, and the argument over this choice persists. The question the episode poses: when a family makes a choice, how much capacity to choose does it actually have?

item.title: Inheritance of acquired traits is proven in nematodes, not yet in humans
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-huberman-获得性遗传在线虫已被证实-人类还没有证据/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-huberman-获得性遗传在线虫已被证实-人类还没有证据/
item.description: Textbooks use the Weismann barrier to explain why the muscles you build can't be passed down; but in nematodes, knock out the offspring's own ability to make small RNAs and they still resist viruses their parents met — change only the RNA in the brain and you change behavior three generations later.
item.content:encoded:
Textbooks use the Weismann barrier to explain why the muscles you build can't be passed down; but in nematodes, knock out the offspring's own ability to make small RNAs and they still resist viruses their parents met — change only the RNA in the brain and you change behavior three generations later.

35 minutes walks the whole conceptual chain from DNA to small RNAs, with the experimental designs and key numbers included; on the mammalian part the speaker repeatedly states what is unknown, so it won't hand you a conclusion you can apply.

4:37 The genome is the whole book, and each cell pulls out one page
Every cell carries the same genome. Rechavi's metaphor is that every room holds an IKEA manual with instructions for building everything in the house; but the kitchen needs different things than the bathroom, so each cell pulls out one page, and that page is RNA, and the furniture assembled from it is protein. The messenger RNA that actually encodes protein is only a small part of RNA: less than 2% of the genome's sequence encodes messenger RNA, while a great deal of the RNA that gets transcribed does other things, many of which are still not understood. This distinction is the foundation for everything that follows — DNA determines which instructions can be opened, and only then does the question become whether lived experience can rewrite those instructions.

11:35 Two barriers block the inheritance of acquired traits
Why, by default, can't what you learn in life be passed on? Rechavi attributes it to two barriers. The first is the separation of soma and germline: in the 19th century August Weismann proposed what is now called the Weismann barrier — only germ cells can hand information to the next generation, and what happens in the rest of the body should stay in the body; this barrier has been called biology's second law, the first being natural selection. The second is epigenetic reprogramming: genetic material accumulates all kinds of chemical modifications, but in sperm and eggs, and in the early embryo, these modifications are largely erased — roughly 90% in mammals and humans. The reason for the erasure is to return to the original manual, preserving the potential to build all the furniture rather than being locked into the few pieces one room happened to make.

12:46 It was opposed and also wanted, and not for data reasons alone
This barrier theory kept acquired inheritance out of favor for a long time. Rechavi describes two sides: one is the theory, the barrier sitting right there; the other is the atmosphere the controversy itself creates. He gives Schrödinger's 1944 book as an example — Schrödinger wrote that acquired inheritance doesn't hold up and doesn't happen, and at the same time wrote that this is sad, because natural selection is bleak: nothing you do affects the genetic information of the next generation, and all you can give your children is money and education. Rechavi says he can psychologically understand why many people want it to be true, because it gives life meaning. But he doesn't push this into ‘it's promising because people want to believe it’; he only says RNA is a new lead, a candidate molecule that in recent years has come to the fore even in the mammalian field.

16:20 Nematodes can run hundreds of generations in one PhD
Why trust nematodes? The conditions Rechavi lists are concrete: a C. elegans is always 959 cells, 302 of them neurons, and since the 1980s it has had a complete connectome, like a subway map marking who talks to whom; the body is transparent, so you can watch neurons fire directly, and you can switch genes on and off with optogenetics; it was the first animal to have its genome sequenced, earlier than humans; each mother produces about 250 nearly genetically identical offspring, kept in a dish eating bacteria, in a highly controlled environment where nature and nurture can be separated; the generation time is 3 days, so one PhD can run through hundreds of generations of nematodes. Under these conditions, he says, the inheritance of acquired traits in nematodes already has very clear, indisputable evidence, and almost no one in the epigenetics field disputes it.

21:20 Offspring that can't make small RNAs still resist viruses
The experimental design is clean enough to read by color: use a fluorescent virus, and if the virus replicates successfully the nematode turns green, while if it's destroyed it stays black. First let nematodes get infected and clear the virus, then knock out the machinery for making small RNAs in the offspring — these offspring have no ability to make small RNAs from scratch themselves. Then infect them with the same virus. If they still stay black, the only explanation is that they inherited small RNAs from their parents. That is exactly what happens: all the offspring stay black, and the resistance carries on for several more generations. Sequencing can read those small RNAs directly, matching the viral genome, and only offspring whose parents were infected have them. These nematodes have no T cells or B cells; they defend against viruses with RNA, and this mechanism is RNA interference, which won the Nobel Prize in 2006.

24:46 The brain and heredity don't speak the same language
The boldest question in this episode is: can the brain leave information for the next generation? Rechavi points out the obstacle is translation — the brain stores information in the three-dimensional structure of synaptic connections, while any heritable information must squeeze through the bottleneck of a single cell, the fertilized egg. He also offers another possibility: learning something might just mean removing a particular odorant receptor, in which case one RNA controlling that receptor would be enough to pass it on; such phenomena have been reported in mammals, but he says they haven't been proven convincingly enough, because no one has explained how the information gets from the brain to the germ cells. His own route sidesteps the translation problem: in a 2019 Cell paper, changing only the production of native small RNAs in the nematode brain altered the foraging behavior of offspring, affecting them all the way to three generations later, with the mechanism landing on the germline gene sage-2, and also requiring the protein that physically carries RNA.

28:17 Mammals lack an RNA amplifier
Why can nematodes do it while mammals are doubted? The mechanism Rechavi gives is blunt: the nematode's secret is that it can keep amplifying these small RNAs, so the signal doesn't get diluted. In mammals there is no known comparable amplification mechanism, so the question becomes — how does a tiny bit of RNA affect the whole organism? One possibility is that it acts only very early in development: at that point there are only a few cells, and it might even act on the placenta formed during pregnancy, after which development is steered off course step by step, and metabolic problems and the like follow. This is the ‘developmental origins of health and disease’ line of thinking. He also frames RNA's role in mammals as a candidate rather than a conclusion: small RNAs are the leading candidate for transmitting protective or harmful effects of stress, but ‘in mammals we don't know, and time will tell’.

31:07 RNA is more plastic than DNA, so start with diagnostics
The applications come in three layers. The nearest is diagnostics: in Israel, most couples preparing to have children get DNA diagnostics for genetic diseases, but right now no one looks at RNA; if the mechanism were clearer, RNA would be another layer, a whole new world, and there might be certain RNAs associated with disease. The advantage is that it isn't fixed the way DNA is — DNA is yours, and if you can't change it you can only choose another embryo; RNA is plastic. Only a step further out is intervention: in rodent experiments, overfeeding causes problems in the next generation, but if you let the mice exercise, this abnormal inheritance gets corrected; when doing IVF, maybe you could change the RNA composition of the things you introduce. Rechavi is restrained about the timeline: he says this doesn't happen now, it's science fiction, but if it were figured out, he has also imagined telling someone preparing for IVF ‘you should go run on the treadmill for a while’, and that would change your RNA profile.

item.title: Stolen Goods Sell for 70-80% of Retail, and Retail Theft Is Now an Industry
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-oddlots-偷来的货能卖到原价七八折-零售盗窃已经产业化/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-oddlots-偷来的货能卖到原价七八折-零售盗窃已经产业化/
item.description: Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal in stores, and fences clean off the markings and resell, after which the goods go up on secondhand platforms. Networked goods fetch 70-80% of retail; T-shirts and deodorant only 30-something percent.
item.content:encoded:
Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal in stores, and fences clean off the markings and resell, after which the goods go up on secondhand platforms. Networked goods fetch 70-80% of retail; T-shirts and deodorant only 30-something percent.

High information density: Home Depot's head of asset protection breaks down how shrink is categorized, the real P&L of locking up shelves, the pricing patterns of stolen goods, and the progress of federal legislation — with plenty of hard numbers.

8:19 A third of shrink is self-inflicted
Home Depot splits shrink into two buckets: operational/administrative and malicious, which Scott describes as the things we do to ourselves versus the things others do to us. At Home Depot, about 30% of shrink falls into the former, with the rest on the malicious side. The figure that has circulated in the industry for years: of malicious shrink, about 40% is caused by internal employees, 35% by people who walk into the store, and the remainder is self-inflicted operational shrink. These percentages move only within a few points each year, but he believes they are drifting upward, and that it has been underreported ever since COVID — neither police reports nor the FBI's Uniform Crime Report fully capture it.

22:52 Employees are explicitly told not to chase anyone
The bigger problem isn't money, it's people. Scott says professional criminals often use homeless people and addicts to go into stores and steal; these people have one thing on their minds — getting the goods out to exchange for money — so they will fight, and they have fought. People have been injured in Home Depot stores, and some have been killed. So asset protection staff are trained in de-escalation, and the 400,000 store employees are explicitly told not to intervene — just back off. His attitude: he would trade shrink for people's safety every single day, and management and the board would back that decision.

23:53 RFID dies the moment it enters a steel store
Joe asks why RFID has been talked about for 25 years and yet in 2026 is still expensive and hard to scale. Scott says he doesn't understand it either, but explains what's peculiar about Home Depot: it's a hardware store, and the store is full of steel, essentially a Faraday cage, so passive RFID can't be read — you have to use an active-signal approach. He also says tag costs are now almost zero; the real bottleneck is the reading hardware — covering a 140,000-square-foot sales floor with eight separate entrances and exits is extremely costly. They have tried the idea of bricking merchandise before it leaves the store, but retrofitting an entire production line for a single drill is very hard to scale.

25:58 Stolen goods have been pushed onto secondhand platforms
The division of labor works like this: boosters are recruited and given a list, cash, or the promise of drugs to go steal from stores; the goods go to a fence — which might be a garage, a warehouse, or a flea market — who strips the price tags, store markings and electronic tags before reselling, and the money flows up to whoever runs the operation, which might be a small crew of a few people or a transnational gang. After the INFORM Act took effect in 2023, big platforms like Amazon and eBay were required to verify seller identities, so stolen goods shifted to Craigslist and Facebook Marketplace, because the law left a gap that doesn't cover peer-to-peer sellers. Home Depot works backward from the platforms, using models to flag sellers pricing below cost while moving large volumes.

35:19 One combo kit sold means restocking 4.2 times
Whether to lock up shelves is a financial question. Scott says they look at the data: there's a combo kit priced at $799, and for every one sold, they have to restock 4.2 times. Take that to finance and they immediately understand it's a gross margin problem — as long as locking up breaks even or even makes a little money, it's justified. But half of Home Depot's revenue comes from professional contractors, and if they break a bit on the job site, rush to the store and find it out of stock, that's a loss too. So they lock up a carefully selected set of categories, with a QR code to summon an associate, who opens the lock in an average of 90 seconds; and locking up doesn't necessarily hurt sales — in some categories sales actually rise, because the goods are finally there.

39:23 A fake bill of lading can drive the goods right out
In the supply chain he counts three plays: first, pure diversion, where a whole container is rerouted at the port or a transshipment warehouse and taken elsewhere, sometimes even loaded back onto a container ship and shipped away; second, a driver drives eight hours across states, and while he sleeps, someone pries open the trailer doors and moves boxes; third, forging bills of lading and pickup orders, using AI to make the documents look real, and the driver pulls in, says he's there to pick up a certain trailer, and drives off. He says what's new may not be the methods but the volume, because these cases are very hard to pursue. Rail is the area that has clearly worsened over the past five or six years — cars sitting in a yard get pried open by a group; and the other side has good intelligence, they don't touch every car, only the ones carrying guns or electronics.

41:28 AI in security is an efficiency tool
Scott says they have more cases than they can investigate, so for them AI is an efficiency question: a typical organized retail crime case takes an average of 70 days from discovery to closing and handing over to police, and compressing that cycle means they can work more cases. They just replaced the video management system across all 2,300 stores, letting existing cameras run edge analytics — identifying people who linger too long in an area, deliberately avoid associates, or show up where they shouldn't be. He also admits that to identify a particular combination of suspicious behaviors and then recognize a specific person, he doesn't have enough cameras yet, but they will get there. Separately, they have an in-house company doing web scraping.

44:30 Seven years ago nobody cared; now there's a federal bill
He says he's now very optimistic. INFORM is arguably the first federal bill driven by organized retail crime, and next is CORCA (Combating Organized Retail Crime Act): the retail industry broadly supports it, it has bipartisan cosponsors, it has passed the House, it's attached to the NDAA awaiting Senate passage, and the president has said he'll sign it. The rationale is that this crime is inherently interstate — it happens in Cobb County, Georgia, and the goods flow to South Carolina and North Carolina, which is interstate transportation of stolen property, but there were no corresponding federal resources; the bill would provide resources, prosecutors and a coordination center. Seven years ago he was thoroughly pessimistic about this: nobody took it seriously, and the prevailing mood then was decriminalization and defunding the police.

item.title: Baseball's stadium music isn't accompaniment — it's how fans take the game back
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-throughline-棒球场的音乐不是伴奏-是球迷抢回比赛的方式/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-throughline-棒球场的音乐不是伴奏-是球迷抢回比赛的方式/
item.description: Baseball's official historian finds stadium music too loud, but it was fans singing Hey Hey Goodbye in unison that rattled the opposing pitcher — music turns the crowd from spectators into part of the game.
item.content:encoded:
Baseball's official historian finds stadium music too loud, but it was fans singing Hey Hey Goodbye in unison that rattled the opposing pitcher — music turns the crowd from spectators into part of the game.

Medium information density: the first half is baseball music history, and only the second half, the Nancy Faust story, is worth the price. Worth listening for anyone into sports, live experience, or fan culture.

0:00 One walk-up song can turn a passerby into a fan
Host Randa Abdel Fattah says she was indifferent to baseball for most of her life, until Mets pitcher Edwin Diaz's walk-up song Narco in 2022 changed that. Diaz is a closer, usually entering at a key moment in the late innings, and the team uses his walk-up song to announce to the opponent: the show's over, this one's ours. The entrance video went viral, the team started handing out plastic trumpets to fans, the mascots Mr. and Mrs. Met pretended to play trumpets, and eventually the team flew the original artist, Timmy Trumpet, in from Australia to perform live. The host says that if you were in the stands then, the feeling was electric.

6:18 The official historian finds the ballpark too loud
MLB's official historian John Thorne says plainly that he doesn't like entrance music. What he misses is the quiet between half-innings — quiet that lets other sounds ring louder and clearer: the strange sound of a bat hitting a baseball, the same sound when Babe Ruth hit, and when Josh Gibson did; the dull thud of a leather glove catching a fly ball; a coach yelling at a player to keep running and steal second. He thinks nonstop audio, the endless fight for fans' attention, may have robbed a kid who goes to the ballpark to dream of that right.

10:31 Take Me Out was originally a women's suffrage song
The seventh-inning stretch was originally literal: stand up, move your legs, get the blood flowing. It became a musical moment thanks to a 1908 song, Take Me Out to the Ball Game, which was actually about women's suffrage. The protagonist of the original lyrics is Katie Casey, a baseball fan who knows all the players' names, gets upset when the umpire blows a call, and when the score is tight knows what to do — she gets the whole crowd to sing along. From this came a new genre, the "baseball song," which flooded sheet music, cylinder records and 78s in the 1910s.

12:35 The baseball song boom was publishers, not fans
John Thorne points out that the 1910s wave of baseball music was less about fans liking it than publishers liking it — it was essentially a marketing tool to pull people into the ballpark. The evidence is the number of copycats: George M. Cohan released Take Your Girl to the Ball Game almost the same week, followed by imitations like I Want to Go to the Ball Game. But although Tin Pan Alley produced so many baseball songs, large-scale singalongs at actual ballparks remained rare, and John says the main reason was technical: sound systems were too primitive, and before radio took hold, a brass band was still the best accompaniment.

17:47 That 1977 singalong broke the opposing pitcher
On a muggy July night in Chicago in 1977, the White Sox trailed the Kansas City Royals by two. After the White Sox put runners on first and second, someone in the stands started singing Hey Hey Goodbye, the sound grew, more than 45,000 fans joined in, and the announcers had to raise their voices to be heard over the singing. The White Sox then erupted — bases loaded, bases cleared, four runs in — and the other side was forced to change pitchers. As the pitcher walked off the mound, Chicago fans "saw him off" even louder. Nancy Faust says what she was thinking was, "Did I hear that right?" because this wasn't the kind of thing you normally heard at a ballpark — it was more like mockery.

23:51 She gave players songs, fans fed her ideas
In her first years with the White Sox, Nancy Faust still played a set repertoire: the national anthem, Take Me Out to the Ball Game, and the hour when the crowd came in. In her third year she started improvising, playing whatever she saw. When Dick Allen came up, the crowd would leave the restrooms and the popcorn stands, so she played the then-popular Jesus Christ Superstar, and when he hit a home run the place went crazy. Fans sitting around her booth started feeding her ideas: one player had worked at a watch counter, the store closed and he got stuck there, so when he came up she played Does Anybody Really Know What Time It Is. She says she was "the soundtrack to whatever was happening," not just scoring the players.

25:52 An opposing pitcher admitted the singalong shook his confidence
After that 1977 singalong, one opposing pitcher told a reporter: you're standing on the mound, there are men on base, Zisk is in the batter's box, thirty thousand people are singing Kiss It Goodbye, and that shakes your confidence. Nancy Faust later read in a book that players recalling those years said they hated hearing that sound, and flinched when they heard na-na-goodbye. And White Sox slugger Richie Zisk said of those same fans: I don't know whether they come to see us or we come to see them, but I can tell you it fired us up. Nancy's conclusion: I guess I did have an impact, I just didn't know it at the time.

28:56 She can't read music, it's all by ear
Every song Nancy Faust improvised over her career, she did by ear — she can't read music. Hum a few bars of anything and within seconds she'd play it back on the organ. She retired from the White Sox organist job in 2010, White Sox fan and former president Barack Obama personally wrote to congratulate her on her career, and the booth she sat in for decades is now named after her. She still occasionally comes back for special occasions, like Pope Night, playing Gotta Have Faith and Don't Stop Believing.

item.title: Iron Age Ireland had no Celtic invasion, only trade and language
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-ancients-爱尔兰铁器时代没有凯尔特人入侵-只有贸易和语言/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-ancients-爱尔兰铁器时代没有凯尔特人入侵-只有贸易和语言/
item.description: The traditional story says Celts brought iron to Ireland around 500 BC, but archaeology finds almost no trace of incoming migrants — Celtic identity was really a language community that grew slowly out of a Late Bronze Age maritime trade network.
item.content:encoded:
The traditional story says Celts brought iron to Ireland around 500 BC, but archaeology finds almost no trace of incoming migrants — Celtic identity was really a language community that grew slowly out of a Late Bronze Age maritime trade network.

Medium information density, with a long setup in the first half. The real value is in the second half, on Celtic identity, sacral kingship and the Fianna warband, suited to listeners interested in pre-Roman Europe.

2:18 Why the Irish Iron Age is the murkiest period
John Waddell says the Irish Iron Age is the darkest stretch of all Ireland's prehistoric periods, partly because the people of the time practised cremation. In much of Europe people were buried with large quantities of fine grave goods, whereas cremation plus burial destroys a great deal of useful archaeological evidence. So despite very fine metalwork and monuments, the absence of burial evidence makes this history especially hard to read. He also points out that using the phrase "Celtic Iron Age" to describe the period amounts to sticking an ethnic label on an era, adding another layer of trouble to an already complicated story.

9:28 Sea routes connected people rather than isolating them
Waddell repeatedly stresses an underrated fact: in prehistory, waterways were channels connecting people, not barriers. Ireland and Britain are both islands, and people habitually assume islands mean isolation, but coastal routes and river routes were very likely the main means of connection. Before the Romans built their straight roads, travel by water was far easier than travel by land. This means we have consistently underestimated how connected the populations of prehistoric Britain and Ireland were. The Irish Sea itself was a connecting force, and the English Channel linked England to the continent.

10:31 The sacred sites are not by rivers but on high ground
Tristan asks whether Iron Age settlements were all close to rivers and coasts. Waddell's answer is unexpected: famous sites like Tara, Rathcroghan and Navan Fort are not obviously on major routes. Each sits on high ground in its own different way, and these locations may have carried a kind of sanctity since the Neolithic. Tara was already an important burial place before 3000 BC, and its story runs into the medieval period, representing more than 4000 years of ritual activity. The importance of these places comes from accumulated time and religious meaning, not from rivers and sea routes.

15:38 A sacral king who fails or is wounded is deposed
Waddell reads a key concept out of medieval Irish texts: sacral kingship. The king of Tara was not a political strongman; his fundamental duty was to maintain the cosmic order. If a sacral king could not bring good harvests, he was deposed. Another feature was that his body had to be flawless: once a sacral king was wounded, scarred or deformed, he was deposed. Waddell thinks this ritual may eventually be traceable in the archaeology of Britain and Ireland, indicating that in the Celtic era, the pre-Roman period, certain tribal rulers did indeed carry a sacred quality.

21:43 The Celts were not invaders but a language community
The traditional story is that around 500 BC a Celtic-speaking people brought knowledge of iron to Ireland. Waddell says this is wrong. His best definition of the ancient Celts is "people who spoke Celtic languages", not an ethnic or racial definition. Ireland in the pre-Roman period was undoubtedly Celtic-speaking, but archaeology finds almost no evidence of immigrants in the Iron Age or the Late Bronze Age. Instead, from around 1000 BC there is abundant archaeological evidence of trade and exchange between Britain and Ireland, with the Thames, the Rhine, the Rhône, the Saône, the Ruhr and the Danube all serving as great corridors. Trade and exchange means the movement of people, and people carried myths, legends and language with them. The Celtic languages very likely took shape gradually amid this Late Bronze Age surge of connectivity.

31:04 The Banquet Hall is really a ceremonial processional way
On the hill of Tara there is a monument called the Banquet Hall, a pair of very long parallel earthworks. Waddell's colleague Conor Newman established that it was never a banquet hall — it is far too large to be any kind of hall. Standing between the banks, you find you cannot see the world outside, because the banks are still high even in their ruined state. Newman proposed that it was a processional way running from the northern end of the hill to the centre of the summit, used for kingly inauguration rituals. There are gaps in the banks that let the procession look left and right at the burials and other monuments on either side, reminding the man about to be inaugurated as sacral king of the ancestors and predecessors. Waddell compares it to Rome's Appian Way, lined on both sides with tombs.

33:07 Beneath Tara lies a timber circle bigger than Stonehenge
Geophysical survey on the hill of Tara revealed a huge circular timber structure, four to five times the scale of Stonehenge. It was probably built around 2000 BC and at the time would have stood on the hilltop as prominently as Stonehenge, yet today there is no trace of it on the ground — only aerial photographs show the faint outline of the circle. Waddell says this reminds us that large timber circles earlier than Stonehenge are a feature of the prehistoric landscape of Britain and Ireland. Tara's burials have another detail: many of them intersect one another, as if new graves were deliberately laid partly over old ones to connect with ancestral remains, both legitimising one's own existence and conveying some kind of story.

39:22 The forgotten king Dathi and a Swiss myth
Waddell tells of an almost forgotten king, Dathi, associated with Rathcroghan in western Ireland. In medieval legend Dathi was the last pagan king of Ireland, said to have campaigned on the European continent, possibly reaching the foot of the Swiss Alps, and finally to have been struck dead by lightning at the foot of the Alps, with his body carried back to Ireland and buried at Rathcroghan. The story was especially popular in the 19th century, because some people took it as proof that Irish military power reached far overseas. But Waddell says it looks like pure fabrication: there never was an Irish invasion of Switzerland. Dathi most likely only raided Britain occasionally. He was later overshadowed by the more famous warrior Cú Chulainn and gradually forgotten.

item.title: No Irreplaceable Leaders, Only Irreplaceable Luck
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-tyler-没有不可替代的领袖-只有不可替代的运气/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-tyler-没有不可替代的领袖-只有不可替代的运气/
item.description: Diamond says history has no irreplaceable leaders — Genghis Khan just happened to be born when the steppe was at its wettest in two thousand years. But people like Rachel Carson and Resnick really did move things forward by ten or twenty years.
item.content:encoded:
Diamond says history has no irreplaceable leaders — Genghis Khan just happened to be born when the steppe was at its wettest in two thousand years. But people like Rachel Carson and Resnick really did move things forward by ten or twenty years.

Diamond is 89, talking about leaders, geographic determinism, Papua New Guinea and Bach cantatas. Medium information density, but the back half — on environmental optimism and writing method — is where the value is.

1:09 No irreplaceable leaders, only irreplaceable timing
