Diamond's answer to ‘who is the most irreplaceable leader in human history’ is ‘no one.’ Not because leaders don't matter, but because time washes out the differences: Jesus was a charismatic founder, but the Roman Empire of the same period had half a dozen other prophets; Genghis Khan built the largest land empire from China to Poland, but recent research found that the wettest period on the steppe in the past two thousand years fell right around his birth — had he been born twenty years earlier or two hundred miles farther away, we would never have known his name. From this Diamond draws a distinction between two kinds of questions: why you and I speak English right now has its answer in the domesticable plants and animals of the Fertile Crescent, nothing to do with individuals; why Amazon is the way it is today has its answer in Bezos alone.

13:50 Rachel Carson moved environmentalism forward by ten years
Cowen challenges Diamond with the environmental Kuznets curve: once per capita income reaches 28,000, countries turn green on their own — was Carson replaceable? Diamond concedes the movement would have come anyway, but stresses she moved it forward by roughly ten years — the day after Silent Spring was published, a senator announced a government investigation into toxic chemicals. More crucial was her position at the time: in that era a professional scientist writing popular science was seen as ‘selling out,’ and she was not a university professor, so no one could say that of her; she was a woman, wrote like a poet, and would read her drafts aloud to hear them. Diamond says that even Richard Dawkins, the best science writer today, does not write as well as she did.

18:00 The pomegranate juice industry waited five thousand years to appear
Cowen tests Diamond's replaceability thesis with the pomegranate juice industry: without the Resnick family, America would eventually have gone down this road anyway. Diamond says no. Pomegranates were domesticated five or six thousand years ago, but there was never a global pomegranate juice industry, because pomegranate juice is extremely hard to make — cut an orange and squeeze, but the pomegranate's value is inside an extremely hard rind, and the contents are not pulp but small seeds; scale production requires a three-story-tall tower that crushes whole pomegranates rind and all. In 2002 America had 22 pomegranate growers, 21 of them small farmers with no money and no motive. Lynda Resnick put in about two hundred million dollars and waited 18 years before turning a profit. Companies like Coca-Cola and Nestlé would never allow a division to invest 150 million dollars and lose money for 18 years.

29:32 Face-to-face social skill is falling off a cliff
Diamond's advice to a 25-year-old who wants to become influential: learn to talk to people face to face, put down the indirect communication tools. He has done 60 years of fieldwork in Papua New Guinea and watched Chevron bring in international lawyers from Switzerland to negotiate with villagers who had never left their village — the lawyers thought they'd close it in a day, but the agreement reached on day one was met on day two with villagers saying ‘we forgot that agreement, the people who signed it don't count, these are a few other negotiators.’ The villagers had negotiated face to face their whole lives and had far more skill than the international lawyers. Diamond says that over the past 40 to 50 years he has watched social skills degrade, and in his 39-year-old child's generation it is especially striking, because most communication is no longer face to face and people no longer understand each other.

33:54 New Guineans may be smarter than Westerners
Diamond answers ‘yes’ outright, and says some people hate him for it. His argument is that natural selection pushed in different directions: for the past ten thousand years European survival depended mainly on surviving smallpox, tuberculosis, measles and other infectious diseases, which has little to do with being smart; the main causes of death in New Guinea were coping with an extremely difficult environment and coping with other New Guineans — warfare there was constant. So his impression is that New Guineans on average ask more questions and are smarter. He adds that Westerners usually think they are stupid because they use stone tools — but they lack metal tools because agricultural output was far lower, not because of intelligence. Cowen presses him on a Nature paper claiming West Eurasians have gotten smarter since the Stone Age; Diamond says he hasn't seen it, but for more than a century eugenicists have been trying to prove Europeans are smarter, with no evidence.

39:24 The Industrial Revolution happened in Britain because it is an island
Diamond rejects Greg Clark's hypothesis that the British became more patient by intermarrying and lowering their time preference. His explanation is geography: Britain is an island, needs no standing army, and has not been invaded — the last successful invasion was 1066. Not needing an army, it gradually developed democracy, and democracy is a productive form of government. Britain also sits on the Atlantic, and like the Netherlands, Spain and Portugal, it was one of the countries that could spread across the world, because the Atlantic coast was the testing ground for seafaring technology. He notes that in the 1600s Britain cut off its king's head and Parliament became powerful. As for Daron Acemoglu and Jim Robinson's extractive vs inclusive institutions theory, Diamond says he has learned more from Jim Robinson than from any individual in the past 20 years, but thinks they give geography less weight than he does.

44:32 Big business and young people have made him cautiously optimistic
Diamond says that 20 years ago he would have said the most evil and destructive force in the world was big business, which at the time basically did not care about the environment. But over the past 20 years big business has come to care more and more: Walmart leads on sustainable products, Unilever leads on sustainable fisheries, even oil companies. In 1999 the World Wildlife Fund sent him to do an environmental study of Chevron's oil fields in Papua New Guinea; he expected it to be terrible, but found Chevron extremely cautious, because they knew that if they screwed up, New Guineans would sue them and they would not get development contracts for Norwegian oil fields. Another source of optimism is young people: 25 years ago young people did not care about the environment, now they care very much. He gives the odds as 51% good outcome, 49% bad.

47:46 The most important question is not to find the most important question
Cowen asks what the biggest environmental problem is at the global macro level, and Diamond laughs and says this is what makes interviewing Diamond frustrating: his answer is always ‘the most important thing is not to go looking for that one most important thing, because the world is complicated.’ He uses marriage as an analogy: a couple about to marry asks what the single most important thing for a happy marriage is, and the answer is not to look for that one most important thing — you need to get 37 things right, and if you get 36 right but disagree on sex or religion, the marriage breaks. Back to the question itself, he says there are three things we must get right: climate change, inequality, and nuclear risk — including the risk of nuclear war and nuclear winter.

item.title: AI Is a Rounding Error for Ordinary People: Diffusion Takes Fifty Years, Backlash Won't Wait
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-interconnects-ai-对普通人是舍入误差-扩散要五十年-反弹却等不了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-interconnects-ai-对普通人是舍入误差-扩散要五十年-反弹却等不了/
item.description: The Industrial Revolution gave ordinary people cheap clothes and sewing machines; AI so far gives them fun images and better search — the benefits are too indirect, and the political backlash is arriving too fast.
item.content:encoded:
The Industrial Revolution gave ordinary people cheap clothes and sewing machines; AI so far gives them fun images and better search — the benefits are too indirect, and the political backlash is arriving too fast.

An eight-minute short take, not especially dense, but it offers a counterintuitive angle: the biggest risk to AI isn't technical failure, it's that ordinary people can't feel the benefits.

0:00 AI is still a rounding error in daily life
The author spent a few weeks on his honeymoon without touching AI at all, and on returning realised: the points where ordinary people encounter AI are either marginal or confusing. The positive impressions are making fun images and an enhanced Google search; the negative ones are addictive social media algorithms, a friend of a friend hooked on an AI chatbot, and various claims about data centers. Family, food, transport, entertainment — the core of daily life — have barely changed directly. His conclusion: being fascinated by AI is the result of a very small number of people actively choosing it, and only by stepping outside the bubble do you see that what's happening today really doesn't matter that much to most people.

0:00 The Industrial Revolution gave physical things; AI gives indirect benefits
The first Industrial Revolution brought cheaper clothes, cookware, reading material and new livelihoods; the second brought sewing machines, food preservation, indoor plumbing, photography, better light sources, bicycles and electrification — a long list, and a very physical one. The author worries that even if AI's benefits materialise (new scientific discoveries, treatments for rare diseases, sustained economic abundance), they are too indirect: ordinary people won't credit OpenAI or Anthropic with saving their life, because it was their family doctor who told them about the new treatment; and not many Americans will care that OpenAI solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem. He judges that fifty years from now, the daily life of the average American will still look a lot like today.

3:47 AI today is mainly a tool serving elites
Knowledge work is about half the US economy, and for that half AI is already (or soon will be) as foundational as electricity, with rapid agent improvements over the next eighteen months accelerating this. But a transformative, highly productive tool that only lifts half of society is highly unstable. The author cites the "Engels' pause": from 1790 to 1840 British workers' wages stagnated while GDP per capita grew rapidly amid technological upheaval. He argues that if the AI industry itself thinks this is the closest analogy, then backlash from those who don't benefit is reasonable. He also agrees with Doug O'Laughlin's judgment: knowledge-work output explodes while headcount in the tech industry very likely shrinks.

3:47 The backlash isn't rooted in AI, it's Big Tech's old debts
The author splits the political backlash facing AI into two layers: first, the early positive effects are too indirect; second, it is deeply intertwined with Western society's historical grievances against Big Tech. He stresses that the latter merely collided with AI in time — if AI's exponential growth had happened decades after the growing pains of platforms like Google and Meta, the data center issue very likely would never have risen to such a central political position. Solving either one would greatly relieve the pressure and give the industry more time to make the positive case. And AI itself, through doom rhetoric and declarations of mass unemployment, has marked itself as a negative or unsafe technology, making both harder.

3:47 Robots might rescue the narrative for LLMs
The author raises an ironic possibility: if the intelligence explosion from mass-producing large language models spills over into robotics and accelerates the spread of robots in daily life, humans will quickly seize on AI's tangible benefits. This is ironic because many people have been working hard to convince the public that this LLM wave is very different from the general AI progress of the past ten or twenty years. If in the end the same dynamic saves (or largely drowns out) the LLM narrative, that would be funny. He also cautions that the connection between robotics, autonomous driving and the current AI revolution is currently more a matter of storytelling.

3:47 Diffusion takes fifty years; the fight against it won't wait
The author calls the present the first five years of a fifty-year diffusion process, and lays out two simple problems: the positive effects are too indirect, and the political backlash is entangled with Big Tech's history. He judges that the story of diffusion will last far longer than the struggle against it. Young people paying attention today will, within their lifetimes, see powerful AI go from effectively 0% to over 90% full adoption. What truly marks AI's evolution is the kind deeply integrated into enterprises and acting as a personal assistant; it is only just becoming viable, and adoption will be far slower than for easily understood applications like ChatGPT. So continuing to push the technology forward is crucial — the benefits are astonishing but not a given, and there is still a great deal of hard work to do on distributing them widely.

item.title: Grok Bot shipped in a month: a small team hid in a cave, a big team would have micro-decisioned it to death
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-lennys-grok-bot-一个月做出来-小团队躲进山洞-大团队会拖没微决策/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-lennys-grok-bot-一个月做出来-小团队躲进山洞-大团队会拖没微决策/
item.description: Building knowledge work into Cursor isn't obviously wrong, but users can smell three visions sharing one screen — that's shipping your org chart. So Grok Bot started from zero, a handful of people hid in a cave for a month.
item.content:encoded:
Building knowledge work into Cursor isn't obviously wrong, but users can smell three visions sharing one screen — that's shipping your org chart. So Grok Bot started from zero, a handful of people hid in a cave for a month.

The first half is the trade-off detail of product decisions; the second half — that a bot should have its own computer, that automation shouldn't have a UI — is worth more.

0:02 Shipping a hit in a month came from a small team hiding in a cave
Grok Bot didn't start as a tab added to Cursor. It started as a team of "a handful of people" isolated in a corner of the office with a private Slack channel, going from first line of code to an internally usable prototype in about a month. Roman's judgment: with a big team and a 6-to-12-month vision plan, you wouldn't build the thing that actually shipped — because every day is a pile of non-obvious micro-decisions, and a big team drags those decisions to death.

9:07 Not putting it in Cursor is because users can smell three visions on one screen
Building knowledge work into Cursor isn't obviously wrong, and the team discussed it seriously. Roman says the problem with that path is "small paper cuts": the product feels oppressive to non-technical users, plus the brand association. He calls out the competitor approach of "a tab for every new form factor" — users can feel that this isn't one unified vision of work but three visions sharing a screen, like "shipping your org chart." So they decided to start completely from zero.

11:08 Two or three hundred manual onboardings, so tomorrow's mistake doesn't repeat
The team personally onboarded two or three hundred people, including the host. The first few were painful: the computer wouldn't start, the user was visibly confused, and the core team had to sit on that 20-minute call. Roman says the effect of that presence is "that can never happen again" — it has to be fixed tomorrow, because tomorrow you onboard the next person. The pattern lasted about two weeks.

12:08 They deliberately didn't tell users what bots to build
Internally, the "5 to 10 bots each owning a slice" pattern emerged on its own. By the end of the second week, people started promoting a standout bot to primary personal assistant, then making it chief of staff and dispatching tasks to other bots — there was even a screenshot of a user telling a bot it got promoted, and the bot asking whether that came with a raise and a bigger token budget. The team noticed, but deliberately didn't guide it during onboarding, afraid of biasing users; they wanted to see whether outside users would get there on their own. Many did.

14:09 Not showing the thinking is a product stance, not laziness
Grok Bot hides a lot of internal machinery: no tool calls, no step-by-step view of what it's clicking on its own computer, just a Slack-like activity indicator and on-demand stage updates. Roman's analogy: you wouldn't ask a colleague to report second by second which button he pressed and which site he visited. Some feedback did ask for a to-do list and priorities, but nobody wanted long text streams and chain of thought — which confirmed the direction.

19:11 Those three weeks of internal beta were mostly unshipping
From internal beta to public launch was only about three weeks, and Roman says that stretch was "we unshipped a lot": cutting experimental features, moving pseudo-developer visibility tools off the product surface, like interfaces that exposed the model's internal thinking and specific memories. The test was "what is the launch post" — if it can't be written as a convincing launch tweet, it probably shouldn't be built. He also distinguishes "Grok Bot now has" (new buttons, new dropdowns, new integrations) from "Grok Bot can now" (new capabilities); the latter is the right frame.

29:17 Automation shouldn't have a UI; 99% is generated from one sentence
Competitors' automation setup means going into a sidebar, clicking plus, picking a trigger event, picking an action. Roman calls that clunky, and the result is that people rarely actually build automations. Grok Bot's approach is to define it in natural language: tell the bot "remind me every morning at 8," and it should just do it — the user should never see the automation-creation UI. Today 99% of automations on the platform are built that way.

30:17 Two early decisions: everything in the cloud, every bot gets its own computer
Roman credits Grok Bot's success to two decisions that weren't obvious at the time. First, users should never have to think about local versus cloud, whether their computer is on, or whether starting from their phone means connecting to the machine at home — all of it goes to the cloud, and the bot becomes a persistent colleague with its own computer, consistent across every entry point. Second, the bot must have its own computer, because a huge number of tools have no decent MCP or API, and humans never worked through MCP and APIs anyway — they clicked pixels and typed into input boxes.

item.title: Don't Blame the Food for Your Kid's Picky Eating: Fix the Relationship First, Then Talk Nutrition
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-secureattach-孩子挑食别怪食物-先修关系-再谈营养/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-secureattach-孩子挑食别怪食物-先修关系-再谈营养/
item.description: The feeding strategy itself matters less than how you execute it; a parent's own relationship with food is the most effective intervention for their child.
item.content:encoded:
The feeding strategy itself matters less than how you execute it; a parent's own relationship with food is the most effective intervention for their child.

Medium information density, but the "health impact tiers" framework and the practical advice on "neutralizing food" offer direct relief to anxious parents.

5:05 The feeding anxiety starts at the nine-month checkup
Jennifer is a registered dietitian who did nontraditional work in the USDA's SNAP education program and considered herself someone who "knew how to feed a kid." At the nine-month checkup the doctor said her child's weight wasn't keeping up, and she said that moment felt like the rug being pulled out from under her. For years afterward she worked to keep her kids on their growth curves, and her second son showed early signs of extreme picky eating. Standing in the kitchen making lunch, she realized she couldn't be the only parent struggling this much, so in 2019 she started Kids Eat in Color, initially posting feeding tips as a hobby.

12:12 The "don't pressure your kid" research isn't that strong
She says "don't force your kid to eat" is a great slogan, and for some families that one line is enough. But after digging deep into the research on feeding pressure, she believes it isn't as strong as dietitians or feeding experts make it out to be, and parents actually have more room to experiment. The second part of her book specifically addresses "what if the standard approach doesn't work": first give the general advice, then give the alternatives that are considered less ideal but can be executed with reduced risk, which she calls risk reduction.

16:19 Put a small piece of green pepper on the plate five hundred times
The exposure method she teaches parents: put a small slice of green pepper on a plate full of foods the child likes. The goal isn't to get him to eat it, but to desensitize him to the pepper's presence. Maybe after five hundred times he'll sniff it, then lick it, then throw it at his brother, then one day eat it. The precondition is that the child is in a regulated state — if the child isn't soothed, he simply can't try new things, because he's scared by something else. So first get the child calm before he sits down at the table.

23:22 An anxious child has a dry mouth and tight throat, and physiologically can't eat
Sarah adds the neural mechanism: when anxious, the mouth goes dry, the throat tightens, and there may be nausea or stomach pain — these are exactly the signs of sympathetic (fight or flight) activation, while eating requires the parasympathetic rest and digest state. In other words, if every time they come to the table it's with dread and a power struggle, you're physiologically pushing the child in the opposite direction of eating. Play, jokes, and little table games work because they bring the child into that relaxed, connected parasympathetic state, and only then do saliva and swallowing come back.

28:26 A meal can be saved from the worst possible start
She tells of one dinner at her own home: before the parents even got back to the table, the two kids were already fighting, and one slammed the door and went to his room. They let that child calm down on his own in his room while the remaining three ate first. Fifteen or twenty minutes later the child came downstairs and started eating, the whole family was laughing together, and everyone was eating. She says the meal ended with the siblings fighting again, but that moment of connection in the middle was real. So don't hold yourself to perfectionism — there's usually at least one good moment in a meal; find it.

32:28 Sensational headlines can basically be swiped away
The first filter she gives parents: if the headline is sensational, you can almost conclude it's wrong, probably about ninety percent of the content is taken out of context, and when you see it just keep scrolling — don't lose sleep over it. But if it's a real event — say an outbreak of diarrhea one summer, or a specific food recall — then pay attention. What she really wants to give is a tiered framework: the first tier is severe food allergies and insufficient calorie intake (ARFID, extreme picky eating, food insecurity), which can make a child seriously ill or worse, and must be addressed first.

33:29 Protein and fiber are in the second and third tiers, food dyes in the fourth
The second tier is protein; every meal and most snacks should include a real protein food. The third tier is fiber, because fiber trickles down: if a child eats enough high-fiber foods, he'll naturally eat less of the added sugar and added sodium. And food dyes, which grab the most headlines, are in the fourth tier, with a very narrow impact. She says that for the vast majority of children, artificial dyes won't change their health trajectory; for the small number of sensitive children, parents have most likely already figured it out themselves. Removing dyes from the food system wouldn't solve the childhood health crisis either.

43:35 Call it a "cookie," not an "occasional food"
To help parents who don't have a healthy relationship with food, her entry point is "talking about food with facts": call foods by their names directly — this is a cookie, this is a sandwich, this is your chicken, this is your sugar. Don't say "this is an occasional food, this is an everyday food," don't sort your child's food into healthy/unhealthy, good/bad, and avoid moralizing and black-and-white thinking. She says there's no evidence that black-and-white thinking directly causes eating disorders, but research has found that black-and-white thinking is very common in children with restrictive eating disorders, and hearing that "foods are good or bad" gets embedded in their restrictive thinking.

item.title: Making Your Rivals Depend on Your System Is How America Has Won for Three Centuries
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-ilt-让对手依赖你的体系-是美国赢了三百年的秘密/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-ilt-让对手依赖你的体系-是美国赢了三百年的秘密/
item.description: The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they can't live without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.
item.content:encoded:
The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they can't live without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.

Walter Mead breaks America's three-hundred-year winning streak into a five-step strategy and pushes it all the way to China, the Taiwan Strait and AI deterrence. What you get is a durable framework for judgment, not news-cycle opinion.

4:47 Unpredictability is a form of power
‘Unpredictability’ is not madness; it is a modern strategy of power. Mead says post-Cold War American diplomacy held itself up as a pillar of stability by ‘letting the whole world know where America's red lines are’, while Trump profits by doing the opposite: crossing lines, threatening allies, turning commitments into bargaining chips. He saw through a secret of the information age — the marginal cost of lying: the first lie is expensive, the thousandth is nearly free. When Clinton was engulfed by the Lewinsky scandal, he discovered that shame only lives in other people's minds; as long as you keep walking, the dogs bark but the caravan moves on. Trump took that insight to industrial scale. The cost is borne by the American diplomatic system: when the world's number one power turns itself into the unpredictable card, every alliance and rule built on predictability after World War II is coming apart faster.

10:00 The last step of global hegemony is cutting the cord
The Anglo-American maritime order did not win through some single battle but through a five-step playbook: first, an open society on an island — the seventeenth-century Dutch tolerated heretics and Jews, and ideas and capital poured in; then global trade, with Dutch merchant ships sailing the world, so wealthy that even their paintings are full of Turkish carpets and Brazilian parrots; third, while continental powers fought over inland Silesia, you seized India and Canada across the globe. The fourth step is the riskiest: instead of copying Spain and sealing off your colonies, you invite the whole world in to do business, the British navy suppresses pirates, and every merchant ship benefits; Germany and Japan were likewise invited in after the war. Only the last step is the hole card: once the other side cannot do without your grain, your rubber and your shipping lanes, you cut it off — Germany discovered in World War I that Argentine grain and Malayan rubber had all been cut off, and its economy promptly seized up.

16:38 Everything China does is to avoid having the cord cut
Look at China through the same framework and you find Beijing is well aware of its own jugular. Mead says: suppose the mainland blockades Taiwan, and the US counter-blockades from a hundred miles off Taiwan's coast: oil cannot get in, manufactured goods cannot get out, soybean contracts with Brazil and Argentina are voided, and China's economy is strangled alive. He has discussed these things with officials and scholars at Chinese universities, and this worry is always present. So China's energy policy has to be read side by side: on one hand building oil reserves so large they surprise outsiders; on the other, throwing up solar and hydropower while digging as much coal as possible. It is not schizophrenia, it is the same thing: pulling out, one by one, the soft spots of ‘dependence on the outside world’. He also warns the US not to retreat into isolationism — agriculture and AI both need overseas markets to feed themselves.

25:50 Every round of technology dividends needs new institutions to match
Mead starts from the ownership society: at America's founding there were independent farmers with land everywhere, and while a bridge is a fine thing, it means raising my taxes — that trade-off is itself a political education. The railroad era was matched by the Homestead Act, with the government giving land to railroad companies and farmers, and a national market grew out of it; in the twentieth century what replaced the family farm was the single-family suburban house, paired with tax-exempt municipal bonds and highways, becoming a new machine for distributing wealth. Today that machine has run into housing prices: young people cannot afford to live near where they work. His remedy is remote work and autonomous driving. When the commuting radius expands from 40 miles to 75 miles, usable land for housing rises with the square of the radius, and the physical space opened by technology is enough to carry two more generations. But the precondition is filling in the institutional ‘infrastructure’ — he coined the word info-structure, meaning the institutions and regulatory rules that let AI actually land in hospitals and courts.

40:22 Silicon Valley is defecting to the tech Hamiltonians
American foreign policy debate has for centuries been four vocabularies: Hamiltonians want a strong state clearing the way for capital, Wilsonians want to spread liberal democracy, Jeffersonians fear a bigger government, Jacksonians stay isolationist in peacetime and fight to the death when hit. The post-Cold War establishment was a marriage of Hamilton and Wilson, but Trump brought Jefferson and Jackson into the room. Mead says the genuinely noteworthy new species is the Tech Hamiltonian. In the 1990s tech companies loved to say ‘we are a global company, Google has no borders, Washington has no jurisdiction’; AI competition has turned tech into a contest of national destiny. Economic positions changed too: the old multinational car companies wanted borderless labor and markets, while Silicon Valley wants supply-chain and IP security, and even wants its employees patriotic — selling code to China is shameful, and your colleagues will report you outright. The core of business has shifted from the old multinationals to tech nationalists, and this is the underwater current of America's political realignment.

50:00 The power with more equipment fears technological turnover most
Mead has been to Ukraine twice. The first time, at a drone factory, he saw them converting children's toy trucks into ground drones carrying mines to blow up tanks; months later, the progress was unimaginably fast. The battlefield is now a gray kill zone, usually only two or three soldiers operating together, and one of the hardest problems is ‘how to get the wounded out’ — you need to build a ground drone with a metal shield to drag people, with a squad of drones alongside to hunt the enemy drones coming to attack it. He heard of one wounded soldier who took 63 days to be evacuated from the front. The changes flip every six months. The bitterest irony for the US: the power with the most tanks and aircraft carriers is precisely the one that fears this kind of parameter revolution most — existing equipment turns from an advantage into a relocation cost. Russia's Black Sea Fleet has no great battle to fight, yet it is bottled up at home by Ukrainian small boats and drones.

54:16 The new variable most worth watching in the Taiwan Strait is Japan
On whether the mainland will attack Taiwan, Mead's judgment is that Beijing needs a very high probability of success before it is willing to cross the threshold — failure would be catastrophic for the initiator. But between ‘attack’ and ‘do nothing’ there is a long gray ladder: for example, requiring all merchant ships bound for Taiwan to first call at mainland ports for customs clearance, or imposing a soft blockade — actions sufficient to change facts on the ground without triggering an armed US response. The real new variable on the Taiwan board is not America's attitude but Japan. The Japanese have already publicly concluded that if China takes Taiwan, Japanese independence is finished too; they are raising defense budgets, rewriting security doctrine and reshaping the national psyche. Historically Japan turns very fast when faced with a real threat. How steep Japan's learning curve is, and whether Beijing's calculations must factor Japan in, is the key to the Taiwan question in the coming years.

1:10:00 AI actually makes deterrence more credible
Moving Cold War deterrence logic into the algorithmic age, Mead points to a counterintuitive corollary: deterrence succeeds or fails on making the opponent one hundred percent believe that ‘if I do X, you will necessarily do Y, and you can do it and are willing to’. As long as there is a human veto point in the decision chain — ‘I might go soft when the time comes’ — that commitment has a crack in it. Automating part of foreign-policy decision-making and handing it to AI turns retaliation into an executable mechanism that will not hesitate — and deterrence becomes more credible. But this is the doomsday machine problem from science fiction: decisions of civilizational scale no longer require a human to bear the consequences. His own assessment of the question is that it is ‘very interesting and also a bit confusing’, and he does not think the answer has appeared yet.

item.title: ECT Is Not What You Think: A Century of Drift from Back Room to Routine Treatment
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/
item.description: Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects remains incomplete, and social misunderstanding has led to its excessive stigmatization.
item.content:encoded:
Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects remains incomplete, and social misunderstanding has led to its excessive stigmatization.

If your impression of ECT is still stuck on One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, this episode will completely reset it. Hear the real procedure, indications, side effects, and one expert's clinical account.

8:07 The actual ECT procedure
If you or I were to receive ECT, here is how it goes: first a risk assessment and informed consent, then a physical exam, and an overnight fast. The next morning, in the hospital or outpatient clinic, an IV line and two blood pressure cuffs are placed (on the arm and right leg), and EKG, EEG, and EMG are connected. After the anesthesiologist puts you to sleep, the leg cuff is inflated to limit blood flow to the right foot, then a muscle relaxant (such as succinylcholine) is given. Once the muscles are fully relaxed, a bite block is placed, and then a brief electrical current is delivered through electrodes (lasting seconds or even half a second). The goal is not to make you convulse all over, but to induce a generalized seizure, typically lasting 25-70 seconds. Because the muscles are relaxed, you see almost no external movement—the whole process is obvious on the EEG.

14:15 Electrode placement and why the right side
There are several electrode placements: bitemporal (like in the movies), bifrontal, and most commonly 'right unilateral'—one electrode on the right temple, the other on the right side of the top of the head. Right unilateral is used for most people because it has fewer cognitive side effects. Why consider the right side first? Because for about 98% of right-handed people and 70%-90% of left-handed people, language function is in the left temporal lobe. Avoiding left-sided electrical stimulation theoretically reduces language-related memory problems. But right unilateral is slightly less effective than bilateral. During treatment, doctors switch based on side effects and efficacy: if bilateral side effects are severe, switch to right unilateral; if right unilateral is not effective enough, switch to bilateral.

16:20 Seizure threshold and effective dose
The seizure threshold is the minimum amount of current that can induce a seizure. There is no precise measuring device; you start by estimating from age, then try small doses upward until a seizure occurs. But treatment is not just about reaching the threshold—the effective dose is usually 2.5 to 5 times the threshold. For bilateral, 2.5 times is enough, while right unilateral requires 5 times, because unilateral stimulation is harder to achieve the same effect. This dose varies from person to person and must be adjusted by trial and error. If a patient has a treatment where the seizure does not occur or does not last long enough (less than 25 seconds), the doctor may increase the dose and try again. Treatments are typically three times a week, with a full course of 6 to 18 sessions, or even longer.

20:22 We still don't know exactly how ECT works
Why does shocking the brain treat depression and catatonia? Frankly: we still don't fully understand. There are several main hypotheses. One is neurotransmitter changes: after ECT, serotonin, dopamine, and GABA (an inhibitory transmitter) all change significantly. The rise in GABA is itself anticonvulsant, which could explain why the seizure threshold rises and seizures get shorter with consecutive treatments. Second, large fluctuations in hormones such as ACTH, prolactin, and TSH are seen in the hypothalamus and pituitary. Third, ECT promotes neurogenesis, with the key molecule being BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor). But how these changes directly relieve symptoms still lacks a one-to-one mechanism. The mechanisms may also differ for different conditions (depression, schizophrenia, catatonia), and for now we can only continue researching.

24:24 Depression data: far better than first-line antidepressants
For treating severe depression, the key data for ECT are quite strong: most studies report remission rates (complete disappearance of symptoms) of 50%-60%, and response rates (marked improvement) of 60%-90%. In comparison, the maximum remission rate for SSRI antidepressants is only about 40%. ECT also has a rare benefit—it can halve the 30-day readmission rate. This is not to say it should be first-line, nor that it has no risks (relapse or symptom rebound within 6-12 months is still not uncommon); but in patients with treatment-resistant depression and severe suicide risk, these efficacy advantages are hard to ignore.

26:27 Memory problems are the most concerning side effect
The most troublesome side effects of ECT center on cognition and memory. Immediately after the procedure there is brief confusion lasting from a few dozen seconds to half an hour, and for weeks there may be decreased attention and executive function. Interestingly, most cognitive functions actually improve in the long term—possibly due to improvement in depression. The real trouble is memory. Anterograde amnesia (difficulty forming new memories) usually recovers within a few weeks after the course ends, so many people are restricted from driving or making major decisions during treatment. Retrograde amnesia (loss of past memories) is what worries patients more: it typically affects recall of the most recent months or even years before treatment, and in most cases recovers, but in some it is permanent. Bilateral treatment is more likely to cause this problem than right unilateral.

34:55 Catatonia: a frequently misidentified fatal syndrome
Catatonia is often simply classified as a subtype of schizophrenia, but it is actually a psychomotor syndrome that can be triggered by any psychiatric or neurological illness. Patients appear awake, with eyes open, yet are almost completely immobile and mute, and may show posturing, waxy flexibility (an arm placed in a position stays there). Because they cannot eat or drink and are immobile for long periods, they are prone to malnutrition, pressure sores, muscle contractures, and even death. Untreated catatonia can have a mortality rate as high as 20%! The most common treatment is benzodiazepines, but ECT is extremely effective in catatonia from various causes. The girl with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis (the 'Brain on Fire' case) mentioned earlier developed catatonia, and both immunotherapy and lorazepam failed; she ultimately recovered with ECT.

48:36 The biggest bottleneck is not efficacy but access
Dr. Lopez believes the biggest obstacle ECT currently faces is finding a treatment site. His hospital performs over 6,000 treatments per year across two campuses, averaging about 10-12 treatments per patient. But it is not widely available across the US, and many adult and pediatric patients travel across states to seek care, especially in cases of infants, children, and adolescents with catatonia due to autoimmune encephalitis, where finding an experienced treatment team is extremely difficult. Therefore, improving access is his greatest hope. At the same time, doctors in other internal medicine, pediatric, and critical care teams often do not recognize catatonia and do not dare or think to consult ECT; so 'preaching' to non-psychiatric colleagues is also part of his daily work.
