item.description: Fan Shiguang, who shot two seasons of Qianlang (前浪), says most marriages end up lukewarm or worse, and growing old together to the very end is rare as hen's teeth; what we lack most isn't stories, it's money, and the habit of seeing old people as specific human beings.
item.content:encoded:
Fan Shiguang, who shot two seasons of Qianlang (前浪), says most marriages end up lukewarm or worse, and growing old together to the very end is rare as hen's teeth; what we lack most isn't stories, it's money, and the habit of seeing old people as specific human beings.

The first half is the two hosts in conversation, heavy on feeling; the second half is the director interview, packed with killed story pitches and behind-the-scenes detail, and the information density is clearly higher — worth starting from 41:00.

4:08 Five million in inheritance, and the law fights the deathbed wish
An elderly woman with no living relatives died in a Shanghai nursing home. While alive she had made a voluntary guardianship notarisation with notary Li Chengyang (李承阳), but she never wrote a will. Sorting through her belongings, the notary found she had left five million in assets, including a house, cash and bankbooks. She had said orally, many times, that she wanted to donate it to society and not give it to relatives, but that wish had no legal form. Li Chengyang ultimately chose to follow the law and look for statutory heirs, tracing through archives to children and relatives she had not seen in years. There was disagreement inside the notary office too; some colleagues thought the old woman's wishes should simply be respected. The compromise was to propose to the inheriting children that 200,000 of the five million go to a fund helping old people with no one to rely on. The children agreed.

11:55 Whether they slept together decides whether the inheritance can be given
An elderly man with a terminal illness gave voluntary guardianship and his estate to a woman who had cared for him for years and was not a relative — and he had a biological daughter. The notary office argued fiercely over it, and one key point was whether the two slept together: if they did not, the carer was merely a nanny or a live-in housekeeper, and an old man leaving his estate to his nanny was morally acceptable; if there was a sexual relationship, the matter stopped conforming to public morals. The carer was herself married, but had had no contact for years, so in effect the marriage did not exist. So it became an open-relationship question, and the notary office did not want to bear the risk of offending public morals on the basis of such a judgment.

16:02 Old people looking for a partner increasingly don't register the marriage
Li Kangmei (李康美), the subject of episode two, was with Lao Li for eighteen years and never registered the marriage from beginning to end, nor was there a de facto marital relationship. The hosts found this far more common than they had imagined: when old people divorce or lose a first marriage and enter a new relationship, many choose not to marry. They don't necessarily say they love the person deeply; they say they want someone to keep them company, someone to look after them, and behind that is a fairly deep need against loneliness. Lao Li already had a terminal illness at the time, and Li Kangmei's choice was whether to stay to the last moment or leave early because there was no de facto marital relationship.

24:46 Reality TV forces you to pick a side every five minutes
The hosts set documentary against reality TV: much of the tension in reality TV is manufactured, backed by a very strong narrative — knowing, say, that the audience has views about mama's boys, so they fabricate a mama's boy on screen. This destroys the audience's tolerance for the complexity of real intimate relationships: every plot beat, every five minutes, demands a position, and that position must be the morally correct one, then gets projected onto some character, and wherever that character goes you side with him. Documentary works the opposite way: it shows that everyone has it hard, some characters get more screen time and some less, but you can see the difficulty of each one, and quite a few of them appear pixelated and anonymous.

34:20 The older generation says I sleep badly, not I'm depressed
Medical anthropologist Arthur Kleinman found that young people today have a rich psychological vocabulary and can quickly say I'm depressed, I'm anxious, I'm a bit bipolar; but the older generation, even when expressing psychological needs, still uses somatised language — I've been sleeping badly lately, I have a bit of a headache — and won't say I sleep badly because I think too much, that I'm a bit depressed. The hosts explain: in our culture it is easier to talk about physical pain, everyone gets a headache or a cold, there's no stigma; the moment you talk about depression or anxiety, it's a different order of stigma and pain.

43:53 The killed pitch: all she wanted was to play mahjong
Director Fan Shiguang (范世广) told a story he killed himself: the most diligent woman in a hospice ward, whose husband had bladder cancer and not long to live. She took the bus in at seven or eight every morning and left at five or six in the evening, like going to work, but you could see no love on her face — she just asked the doctors and nurses again and again how much longer other people's family members had. Only later did it emerge that her son had died of a heart attack two years earlier; she was a shidu family, and her tears had probably run dry two years before. Someone asked what she wanted to do after her husband died, and she said she wanted to play mahjong, because he had never let her play. The first scene shot after the husband died was her finding workers to smash the legs off a two-metre bed with a sledgehammer, one by one, and buying a mahjong table to put in that spot. The story was never used, because the team could not find her real inner world — they only had hold of part of the facts.

52:28 Growing old together is rare as hen's teeth, not the norm
Fan Shiguang said the team embedded in roughly fifty families during fieldwork, and across the two seasons found that going from youth all the way to growing old together to the very end is not the norm but rare as hen's teeth; most marriages are lukewarm, or worse. He told of the first season's episode Lovers: an old man with Alzheimer's loses control and hits his wife, the daughter forcibly sends him to a specialised nursing home, and the old woman sneaks off to visit every few days, though the hospital won't let her come because it affects his mood. After the old man is hospitalised, gravely ill, the old woman finally gets her chance to wait on him — cutting his nails, washing his hair, washing his feet. More than a month after he died, she said through tears: I looked down on him my whole life. When I was young I was a good student and he was a poor one, my family were intellectuals and his were workers, he insisted on courting me, I had no way out, and in the end I muddled through a whole life with him.

1:04:18 Learning to drive at 95: one sentence strips away the right
Fan Shiguang said the team worked hard to break stereotypes, because people love to sort others into groups and stick labels on them — old people are like this, they've gone senile — and there is deep prejudice in that. In season one there was the story of a 95-year-old man learning to drive and taking the licence test; he caught himself saying, offhand, "driving is all very well, but he is 95 after all", and then asked himself: in that sentence of mine, a 95-year-old has in fact been stripped of his rights — that is, he doesn't deserve them. No Ministry of Public Security law or regulation says a 95-year-old cannot learn to drive, but in our verbal violence the right was stripped away. The episode's bullet comments were full of people saying can this old man really be allowed on the road, how selfish, what if he hits someone — and all those worries rest on prejudice.

item.title: The Supreme Court Gave Students Constitutional Rights, Then Handed Searches and Paddlings Back to the Schools
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-stuffmissed-美国最高法院先给了学生宪法权利-后来又把搜包和体罚还给校园/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-stuffmissed-美国最高法院先给了学生宪法权利-后来又把搜包和体罚还给校园/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: From refusing to salute the flag to searching backpacks, six cases gradually drew the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Supreme Court declared that schools are not totalitarian enclaves while also upholding corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion searches, narrowing the boundary of those rights.
item.content:encoded:
From refusing to salute the flag to searching backpacks, six cases gradually drew the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Supreme Court declared that schools are not totalitarian enclaves while also upholding corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion searches, narrowing the boundary of those rights.

Each case gets five or six minutes laying out the background and the holding, suited to listeners who want to grasp the boundaries of speech, corporal punishment and searches in American public schools in one sitting.

5:10 The flag-salute case: student rights enter the schoolhouse for the first time
Can students really invoke the First Amendment during class? This case actually begins with religion: Jehovah's Witnesses families held that saluting the flag violated the commandments against having other gods and against graven images, and refused to pledge or salute the flag. In 1940 the Supreme Court had ruled against them, and World War II led more school districts to require students to salute and recite the pledge of allegiance daily. West Virginia expelled students who refused the pledge, labeled them delinquents, and their parents could be fined or even jailed. In 1943 the Supreme Court overturned the earlier ruling 6 to 3, and Justice Jackson wrote the opinion on Flag Day: orthodoxy in politics, nationalism, religion or other matters of opinion is not to be defined by any official; students need not utter words they do not believe, nor make empty gestures. This was the first time the Court established that students possess some First Amendment rights inside school.

11:21 An official prayer is ruled unconstitutional
In the Cold War the United States cast itself as a God-fearing nation, added Under God to the pledge of allegiance in 1954, and more public schools began reading scripture or praying before class. In 1951 the New York State Board of Regents asked religious leaders to co-write a short interfaith prayer, and each district decided whether to adopt it. Districts that used the prayer allowed students to opt out, but the parents of 10 students still sued. In 1962 Engel v. Vitale ruled it unconstitutional 6 to 1; the key was not whether it was compulsory but that the prayer was written by the government, which itself constituted an establishment of religion. Justice Black quoted Madison: it is proper to take alarm at the first experiment on our liberties; the same authority that could establish Christianity to the exclusion of other religions could easily establish one Christian sect. The ruling provoked fierce backlash, and the plaintiff families were mocked and harassed.

18:31 An armband is constitutional expression
In December 1965, middle and high school students in Des Moines planned to wear black armbands to class to protest American involvement in the Vietnam War. School officials announced in advance that refusal to remove them would mean suspension, and some students — including four siblings — wore the armbands anyway and were suspended. In 1969 the Supreme Court ruled for the students 7 to 2. The issue was that this was not ordinary dress or grooming but quiet, passive expression close to pure speech, and it did not disrupt class. Absent evidence of actual or demonstrable substantial interference with teaching, school officials may not suppress student opinion. The ruling said: public schools may not be totalitarian enclaves, and students and teachers do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate. This substantial disruption standard later became the baseline for free speech on campus. Justice Black dissented that students would from then on resist almost every school rule, and the host says on the show that this slippery-slope argument sounds rather absurd.

24:40 A school-funded newspaper can be censored
In 1983 two pieces in the Hazelwood East High School student newspaper The Spectrum troubled principal Reynolds: a story about teen pregnancy used pseudonyms but the interviewees might still be identifiable, and a story about divorce named and criticized a student's parent. Reynolds decided to cut both entire pages rather than just remove the articles, on the grounds that there was no time to revise and the paper had to come out before the semester ended. In 1988 the Supreme Court ruled for the school 5 to 3. The key distinction is between tolerating student speech and promoting it: this newspaper was funded and published by the school, readers would take its contents as endorsed by the school, and the two pieces were indeed immature by journalistic ethics. The Court held that school officials may exercise control over the content they promote. The rights established in Tinker were thus given their first clear boundary.

29:46 Corporal punishment is not an Eighth Amendment matter
Host Tracy suddenly recalls that many teachers kept wooden paddles on their desks when she was a child, and on looking it up finds that corporal punishment has still not disappeared in the United States. In the 1977 case Ingram v. Wright, the school's paddle was under two feet long, three or four inches wide and half an inch thick, in principle one to five swats; but Ingram was struck more than 20 times in a single incident and needed medical attention. The Supreme Court did not dwell on whether that individual case was excessive but held that school corporal punishment does not violate the Constitution. The reasoning is that the Eighth Amendment protects those convicted of crimes, and prisoners are separated from schoolchildren by the harsh facts of criminal conviction and imprisonment; schools are open places, with teachers and classmates as witnesses, and students go home at the end of the day. According to NEA figures, corporal punishment remains legal in public schools in 17 states and is actually practiced in 14, and boys, Black students and students with disabilities are paddled at significantly higher rates.

33:52 Searching a backpack needs only reasonable suspicion
In 1980 a 14-year-old student known as TLO in New Jersey was reported by a teacher for smoking in the restroom. Vice principal Choplik searched her purse, saw cigarettes and rolling papers and kept looking, found what appeared to be marijuana and evidence of drug dealing, and TLO was ultimately convicted and sentenced to a year's probation. In 1985 the Supreme Court upheld the search 6 to 3. The ruling acknowledged that the Fourth Amendment binds school officials and that students have a privacy expectation, but that it must be balanced against the school's need to maintain a learning environment. So school searches need not meet the probable cause required of police, only the lower threshold of reasonable suspicion. The teacher's report that TLO was smoking gave the vice principal reason to suspect she had cigarettes, and a purse is exactly the obvious place; seeing rolling papers naturally extended the suspicion to marijuana, which was equally reasonable.

item.title: To Make Criticism Land, Lead With High Standards and Trust
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-thinkfast-批评想被听进去-先给高期待与信任/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-thinkfast-批评想被听进去-先给高期待与信任/
item.description: Getting criticism believed isn't about opening with a few compliments — it's about letting the other person see that the standard is high and that you believe they can reach it. In one experiment, a single line — "the standard is high, but I know you can meet it" — pushed Black students' rate of revising their essays to the highest of any condition.
item.content:encoded:
Getting criticism believed isn't about opening with a few compliments — it's about letting the other person see that the standard is high and that you believe they can reach it. In one experiment, a single line — "the standard is high, but I know you can meet it" — pushed Black students' rate of revising their essays to the highest of any condition.

The originator of stereotype threat research breaks down the mechanism himself and grounds the intervention in a replicable experimental script. Twenty minutes of high information density, with none of the vague communication-tips pablum.

1:04 Identity bias makes people underperform on the spot
When a situation carries a negative label about one of your identities, and that situation matters to you, you worry about being judged by that label. That worry comes from the situation itself: it depresses performance on tests, sports or intellectual tasks in the moment, and it makes people chronically avoid such situations over time — which in turn shapes who they befriend, where they live, and where they send their kids to school. The anxiety doesn't come from ability; it comes from the expectation of being defined by the label.

3:10 Social media surrounds you with labels
Social media's power lies in how fast it spreads thumbnail sketches of what a group is like. People have no patience to see the full picture and the exceptions, so it naturally multiplies the number of situations in which you might be seen through your identity. Occasionally it also spreads images that reduce threat, but the overall tone skews negative — the result being that in a diverse society, everyone is more on guard about their own identity and about what others might be thinking.

6:16 A 15-minute self-affirmation exercise raises grades
In racially integrated classrooms, Black students live with the constant possibility that their ability is being underestimated. Teachers asked seventh graders to spend just 15 minutes writing a short essay about the people and things they valued most. White students were barely affected, but Black students used the occasion to let the teacher know "I'm not just that label," and their grades began to rise — setting off a positive feedback loop: better grades → less vigilance about the label → still better grades. The intervention cost almost nothing, yet it changed long-term trajectories.

9:20 Vigilance in diverse settings: remember or forget
The author calls this state churn. In settings where people of different backgrounds are together and the outcome matters, people are pulled back and forth between two options: remember that "others might read me through my group's stereotype" in order to protect themselves, or simply forget it, relax, and trust the person in front of them. This isn't fragility; it's the real pressure the situation imposes. When the setting matters, it continuously drains attention that should be going to the task.

12:24 High standards plus trust make feedback work
In the experiment, students wrote an essay about a favorite teacher and received critical feedback. The first two ways of giving it — straight criticism, or criticism preceded by a "positive buffer" — were trusted by white students and deeply distrusted by Black students. The third way added only one sentence: "We have high standards, because these essays will be published; I read your essay and I believe you can reach them." Under that condition, Black students took their essays home to revise at three times the rate of the other conditions.

14:26 You can't assume others already trust you
After years as a dean and provost, Claude considers the most useful skill to be realizing that everyone you work with needs that signal of respect. Society's common mistake is to assume trust is already there, when in reality people worry about how you view the group they belong to. Truly effective leaders are good at giving that signal first: even if an employee disagrees with a decision, as long as they feel the other person respects who they are and their potential, the team atmosphere is completely different.

17:35 Let people see you're human before you talk trust
Claude breaks good communication into three things: first, let the other person know you understand what this situation means to them — when power is unequal, the person with more power has to send the safety signal first; second, near-obsessive clarity, because beating around the bush destroys valuable information; third, warmth and goodwill, because people need to confirm that the person across from them is a good person before they hand over trust. Matt sums it up as connection, clarity, care.

item.title: Latin Doesn't Make Surgeons: Exams Should Be Hard at Something Useful
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-econtalk-拉丁文练不出外科医生-考试难-不如考得有用/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-econtalk-拉丁文练不出外科医生-考试难-不如考得有用/
item.description: Latin doesn't make surgeons: skills barely transfer. If you assume harder material sharpens the mind, a nation's brightest get wasted on the most useless knowledge — that is the lesson of the Qing examination system.
item.content:encoded:
Latin doesn't make surgeons: skills barely transfer. If you assume harder material sharpens the mind, a nation's brightest get wasted on the most useless knowledge — that is the lesson of the Qing examination system.

It puts imperial civil-service exams, military selection and modern transfer experiments on one chain of evidence, unusually connecting history with talent assessment — and the two sides genuinely clash.

10:03 The exam content was wrong, and clever candidates couldn't save the state
Hong Xiuquan failed the Qing examinations at least four times. After his last failure, he had visions on the road home, came to believe he was the younger brother of Christ, and eventually launched the Taiping Rebellion — which Daisy says may be the deadliest civil war in human history, with deaths perhaps around thirty million. He was not alone: examination seats fell far short of the number of candidates, many sat the exams into their forties and fifties without passing, and the only way home was to teach. Daisy adds that the deeper cost fell on those who did pass: they were masters of the eight-legged essay yet knew nothing of the science and mathematics transforming the world. When the brightest young men can only rehearse a dead format, the country bleeds from both ends.

22:51 British civil-service reform was elites reproducing themselves
The Northcote-Trevelyan report is often seen by the British as the founding document of the modern civil service, but Daisy backs the revisionist reading: in the name of a unified exam, it pushed Oxford and Cambridge classics graduates into key posts. Benjamin Jowett, master of Balliol, worked behind the scenes to place his classics students throughout the empire. Michael Coolican's "No Tradesmen and No Women" points out that the 1854 report reduced the most brazen buying and selling of offices, but also snuffed out the professional exams that departments had been growing. Exams can select people; what they examine decides whether they select the worthy or select people like themselves.

35:58 A bureaucracy without price signals corrects itself through corpses
Daisy attributes bureaucratic failure to the absence of feedback: no price mechanism, no profit and loss, so a department cannot tell whether its plans save lives or destroy them. The military sounds like a counterexample, but military bureaucracies err just as constantly in peacetime; almost every time Britain went to war after a long peace, a crisis brewed in the first year — the shell crisis of early World War I being one. What actually forces correction is not internal inspection but mass death on the battlefield. She calls it a corrective mechanism crueler than prices. To make a bureaucracy reliable, you must first create a signal that shows consequences; otherwise no severity of selection can save the quality of everyday decisions.

43:06 The Royal Navy won by examining navigation, not Latin
Daisy notes that the real pillar of Victorian Britain was not the army but the Royal Navy. As early as 1677, after a run of defeats by the Dutch, Samuel Pepys introduced an oral exam for captains: three senior officers questioned a candidate face to face on how to command a ship. Over the following century and more, navigation, charting and trigonometry entered the written exams, and chart-makers like Nelson, Cook, Flinders and Bligh passed through that gate. Daisy draws out two exam traditions: Pepys tested skills needed immediately; Macaulay and Northcote-Trevelyan later wanted classical languages. One served safety at sea, the other a barrier of status, and the results differed accordingly.

47:31 Content doesn't matter? Macaulay's screening argument is missing a link
Here comes the highlight: Daisy reads Macaulay's 1833 parliamentary speech aloud. The gist is that whatever a age happens to teach, those who excel at it must be the cleverest, most industrious and most honor-seeking of the young; so Cambridge could teach Ptolemy instead of Newton and its top students would still be excellent; teach Cherokee instead of Greek and the best Cherokee scholars would still be the best men; even astrology and alchemy would do. Another MP praised it on the spot as the most practically wise speech in parliamentary history, but Daisy says flatly: this is eloquence running away with its author, and it misses entirely that what you learn really does matter.

51:21 Dead twigs and corn: wrong content makes discipline just watering
Daisy closes out Macaulay with the 1917 rebuttal of the American medical educator Abraham Flexner. Flexner said the devotees of mental training resemble Egyptian priests: they plant a row of dead twigs in the soil and then water them on schedule for the sake of discipline. Plant corn and the discipline is no less, with a crop thrown in. Against the American medical schools of the day, where many aspiring doctors were forced through Greek and Latin before they could touch a medical book, Flexner's answer was: medicine is already hard enough, and using it to sharpen the mind is far more efficient than using dead languages. Daisy agrees: spend the best years of the most gifted on what has been disproved or is useless, and the winners will be rivals who let their young learn real knowledge.

59:21 Rectangles don't train triangles: transfer needs identical elements
Thorndike designed a cleaner controlled experiment: have people repeatedly estimate the area of rectangles until they clearly improve, then have them estimate the area of triangles — almost no transfer. If even two shapes this close show nothing, the claim that classical languages sharpen the mind is even less credible. Thorndike's explanation was identical elements: transfer appears only when old and new tasks share the same components; far transfer essentially breaks down. Daisy draws the exam-design principle from this: to select people who can navigate, examine navigation and trigonometry; to select people who can practice medicine, examine medicine. An exam that actually works wires its difficulty directly into the real task.

item.title: Global Liquidity Peaks: The More Aggressively a Company Spent on AI in H1, the Sooner It Gets Discounted
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-cn38ff4a-全球流动性见顶-上半年越激进砸-ai-的公司-越先被折价/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-cn38ff4a-全球流动性见顶-上半年越激进砸-ai-的公司-越先被折价/
item.description: A rising capital market requires new money to keep buying in. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that were most aggressive on AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.
item.content:encoded:
A rising capital market requires new money to keep buying in. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that were most aggressive on AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.

It puts US AI capex, Hong Kong IPOs and household balance sheets on the same funding chain — a macro framework that does not treat AI as a panacea.

0:33 A low IPO break rate is not a good signal
Do not read Hong Kong's low first-day break rate as a sign of market strength. In the first half of this year the break rate was only in the teens, far below the roughly fifty-fifty level that a market-based mechanism would produce. That means the main participants in these IPOs are short-term speculative arbitrage funds, not long-term investors. Recently the supply of new listings has shrunk and IPO-related funds have blown up, yet the two most recent listings still broke issue, showing that temporary supply-side controls have not solved the underlying problem: Hong Kong also faces peak liquidity.

12:07 The more aggressive on AI, the sooner punished
Market attitude reversed within a single quarter. Before Q1, the capital market rewarded aggression: the louder the AI CapEx, the higher the valuation. By late July, when half-year reports were disclosed en masse, any large internet company that had made aggressive capex in the first half — especially those that burned through free cash flow — was discounted, and even Google was not exempt. Q2 was precisely the quarter of maximum FOMO across the entire supply chain, with everyone rushing to spend before prices rose, and inventories still propping up gross margins. By Q3, inventories are depleted and the impact of price increases returns, so the negative factors will show up together.

15:54 Nvidia is closer to Cisco in 2000
Nvidia's earnings look good, but its cash flow is changing. Before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, Cisco rolled out 'lease-to-buy' to help customers finance purchases, pulling future revenue forward into current sales. Nvidia is now also pushing lease-to-buy. In its financials, free cash flow halved quarter-on-quarter, and accounts receivable are far above historical levels — speculated to be partly related to the credit enhancement and collection structure that lease-to-buy brings. So Nvidia may have reached a stage where it needs more aggressive financial engineering to sustain capital-market expectations, similar to Cisco's situation back then.

33:21 Primary-market money comes from bullets fired three years ago
The answer lies in fund-raising timing. The money that will be deployed heavily into AI and robotics from H2 2025 to H1 2026 mainly comes from funds raised at the market peak in 2020-2022; they barely invested in 2023-2025, until they saw state capital placing bets when no one dared and earning the most — the stories of ChangXin and ChangCun, two large models, and two large chips stimulated market-based capital. The mindset is: copy the state capital's homework. So this is not a rational long-term incremental wave, but more like a delayed emotional release.

47:31 Property policy removes households from the financing chain
The key to recent real estate policy is not bailing out developers, but pulling households out of the old financing loop. In the past, buying a pre-sale home meant the household played the role of financing target in the investment-driven chain: pay first, receive later. The policy pushes the chain toward marketization, so buyers get completed homes and only bear the consumer role, with risk reset back to developers and financing institutions. The policy was introduced when home prices were near the bottom to first stabilize the denominator on the asset side, avoiding panic from dismantling the chain during a downturn. Japan after the 1990s and China's coal and mining consolidation followed similar paths.

1:01:34 A slow bull is not a slogan, it is chip structure
A slow bull does not rely on slogans; it relies on layering market chips by duration. At the bottom are low-valuation, high-dividend blue chips held by insurers as long money that rarely trades. Above that are mutual funds and index funds, performing a quasi-stabilizing function. Central Huijin and China Securities Finance adjust the index at a higher layer. At the top are retail investors, private funds and active managers. New insurance regulations require liabilities and assets to match in term, yield and liquidity, effectively ensuring long money invests long, medium money medium, and short money short — no using ordinary people's short money to invest in ten-year illiquid assets.

1:22:49 Crises get bigger with each rescue, bubbles at least one and a half
After the US dollar left gold in 1971, global central banks became increasingly accustomed to printing money to directly intervene in crises, acting faster each time. The quantitative easing after 2008 should have been cleared during a rate-hiking cycle, but was interrupted by political intervention, and then came the pandemic in 2020, so a larger wave of easing was layered on top of a bubble that had not yet dissipated — today we have accumulated at least one and a half bubbles. Central bank governors have learned to print more money immediately when a crisis appears, and the endogenous result is simultaneous increases in inflation, financial asset prices and wealth inequality. As long as bubbles are not allowed to clear, the world may face long-term stagflation in some form.

item.title: Central Banks Won't Kill the $100 Bill: It's a $2.5 Trillion Interest-Free Loan
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-oddlots-央行不愿废除百元美钞-那是一笔-2-5-万亿无息贷款/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-oddlots-央行不愿废除百元美钞-那是一笔-2-5-万亿无息贷款/
item.description: Cash use keeps falling, yet currency in circulation keeps hitting records. Central banks have an incentive to keep printing $100 bills: the money is effectively a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the U.S. government, and the price is convenience for money launderers worldwide.
item.content:encoded:
Cash use keeps falling, yet currency in circulation keeps hitting records. Central banks have an incentive to keep printing $100 bills: the money is effectively a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the U.S. government, and the price is convenience for money launderers worldwide.

It strips money laundering back from "bank wires" to watches, tractors, casino chips and VAT loopholes, and explains why central banks can't bear to kill the $100 bill.

5:09 The scale of money laundering hasn't changed in thirty years
The most commonly used estimate of money laundering is 2% to 5% of global GDP per year, which at today's roughly $100 trillion GDP is $2 trillion to $5 trillion. That figure comes from a rough estimate by former IMF managing director Michel Camdessus in the late 1990s, and no one has come up with a better answer since. Oliver warns that the more alarming thing is that this ratio hasn't moved in thirty years: decades of anti-money-laundering action have not shrunk the criminal economy, only barely held it back from growing faster than the overall economy.

9:10 Banks spend $200 billion a year on AML for near-zero effect
Banks complaining that KYC is too expensive isn't just whining. The U.S. passed the Bank Secrecy Act in 1970, and in 1989 the FATF turned anti-money-laundering into a global norm, forcing banks to hire compliance teams and install AI monitoring software. LexisNexis estimates global AML compliance costs about $200 billion a year, enough to solve world hunger and provide clean water to everyone. Yet the system generates enormous numbers of suspicious activity reports every year, and launderers still run ahead of regulators. The problem isn't that banks aren't trying; it's that the whole system is expensive, weakly feedback-driven, and almost no one is accountable for outcomes.

12:14 Trade-based laundering is an order of magnitude bigger than cash smuggling
Cash smuggling makes laundering inside the banking system look small, but the bigger chunk never touches money at all: value is hidden in goods. About $25 billion in cash flows into Mexico each year, while John Deere and Caterpillar farm equipment exported from the U.S. becomes the consideration cartels get back; European luxury goods flow to China, and drugs and goods are imported back in the China direction, with the triangle settled through misinvoiced documents. Global Financial Integrity estimates this kind of trade-based laundering at about $1 trillion a year. A million-dollar watch worn through customs is far easier than moving a million in cash.

17:18 The Vancouver model: Chinese cash demand meets cartel supply
Each person in China has only a $50,000 annual foreign-exchange quota, while wealthy Chinese have plenty of demand to spend abroad. The Vancouver model matches that demand with cartels' dollar cash supply: bags of cash outside Canadian casinos are handed to Chinese gamblers, the money is lost at the tables, and the gamblers run up gambling debts; that debt is offset on the other end in China by an RMB transaction and by drug sales that flow in afterward. Looked at as just the gambling, it looks like a loss; looked at across the whole chain, it is a triangular settlement that simultaneously repatriates cartel money and moves Chinese capital out. The model later spread worldwide, with luxury goods, consumer goods and drugs all serving as vehicles for moving value.

23:25 The VAT loophole lets the same goods extract 20% over and over
Zero-rated cross-border transactions in the EU were meant to keep national tax authorities from having to audit each other, but they became an ATM: goods entering the UK from Ireland need not pay VAT, and when sold to an affiliated shell company 20% is added; that shell company re-exports the goods back to Ireland and can claim a refund from UK tax authorities of the 20% that was never paid. The loop repeats, hence carousel fraud. The UK once largely suppressed it with a multi-agency crackdown, and the fraudsters then moved to continental Europe, where it now runs about €50 billion a year, spreading from Lithuania all the way to Portugal. Criminal organizations have no ceiling on cooperation: the more they cooperate, the bigger they get.

27:27 Nobody uses cash, yet central banks are printing record notes
In the digital-payments era, cash is down to about 9% of transactions in the UK and about 13% in the U.S., so by ordinary logic the supply of paper money should be shrinking. After Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey raised the banknote paradox in 2009, the phenomenon only intensified: the value of UK notes in circulation doubled, and the U.S. is near $2.5 trillion. Central banks blaming "store of value" doesn't hold up — surveys show the average American adult carries only a bit over $400, while per-capita U.S. currency in circulation works out to more than $7,000. The Fed estimates about 65% of U.S. bills are abroad, but that just pushes the question past the border: no one knows whose hands these notes are actually in.

32:31 The $100 bill is a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the government
Seigniorage can't simply be understood as the profit from printing money: a $100 bill costs 9 cents, but it isn't "sold" to you — you can always exchange it back for goods at face value, so the cash the public holds is essentially an interest-free loan. With nearly $2.5 trillion in U.S. currency in circulation, the U.S. government gets interest-free funding equal to about 6% of the national debt; federal interest payments are now about 19% of the budget, and if that $2.5 trillion also had to pay interest, that would add roughly another percentage point. This is exactly why central banks don't want to hear talk of abolishing cash.

47:51 AML incentives are inverted: the more reports, the less crime gets policed
Suspicious activity reports were meant to be real-time intelligence for law enforcement, but reality is the exact opposite: banks hire thousands of compliance officers to fill out reports, law enforcement has no resources to read them, and most reports fall into a black hole; a bank that misses a report can face billion-dollar fines, while getting it right earns no reward. Side effects include debanking — large numbers of people who come under suspicion, many of them Muslim, get cut off from financial institutions. The guest's solution isn't to hire more compliance officers but to generate fewer reports, actually read them, and genuinely prosecute financial criminals, raising the cost of money laundering instead of drowning everyone in paperwork.

item.title: Russia Is Stuck in Ukraine, but Still Has Room for a New Front Against NATO
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-hiddenforces-俄罗斯陷在乌克兰-仍有余力对北约开新战线/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-hiddenforces-俄罗斯陷在乌克兰-仍有余力对北约开新战线/
item.description: Russia has not won in Ukraine, but attrition has forged the world's most advanced drone-infantry combat experience; the guest argues it has ample capacity for a limited probe against NATO, and the window is the final phase of Trump's term.
item.content:encoded:
Russia has not won in Ukraine, but attrition has forged the world's most advanced drone-infantry combat experience; the guest argues it has ample capacity for a limited probe against NATO, and the window is the final phase of Trump's term.

The guest is the Wall Street Journal's chief diplomatic correspondent, and was in Kyiv on the day of the 2022 invasion; his judgments on Russian military capability and Europe's fractures are far more concrete than those of TV commentators.

19:16 Trump's anti-Europe talk may be taken literally by Putin
Everyone is guessing whether John Ratcliffe's secret trip to Russia was there to negotiate terms. The guest's judgment is that the visit looks more like carrying a message to Moscow on Trump's behalf: don't take those on-air remarks about America not caring about Europe seriously — if Russia invades Lithuania, Estonia or Finland, the US will send troops. The reasoning is that Moscow is bogged down in a war of attrition in Ukraine and badly needs to cut off European support for Ukraine, so escalating with a probe against NATO is one option, while Trump's earlier statements that Europe is a bunch of freeloaders gave Putin room to misread, hence the need for a dedicated trip to make the red line clear. One caveat: the guest does not have intelligence from inside that room; he is explaining why the account is entirely plausible, not confirming it.

21:27 Russia's army isn't spent — it can still open a limited front
Russia has been unable to take Ukraine for a long time — does that mean it cannot open another front? The guest's answer is blunt: it can absolutely open a limited front — not tanks rolling across Poland to Paris, but something in the Baltic direction, such as blocking the narrow land corridor of the Suwalki Gap. He says the Russian and Ukrainian armies are the only two in the world today that fight modern drone-infantry warfare as a daily routine. The story of a 20-person Ukrainian drone team destroying an entire traditional battalion circulates widely, but the Russian military has the same technology in hand: 20 Russians can likewise wipe out a NATO battalion that has not trained against drones. Outsiders assume Russia grows weaker the longer it fights, and overlook that it is also one of the parties tempered by this technological revolution.

22:31 NATO might not even save Lithuania from Poland
A war game designed to simulate a Russian invasion of Lithuania led the guest to a deeply unsettling conclusion: even Poland did not send troops to save Lithuania, let alone other allies. The reason is not a lack of military capability, but that Russian forces advance too fast and nuclear deterrence hangs over everything, so allies fall into hesitation over whether to enter, producing a chain of waiting and watching. The guest says Moscow has factored exactly this into its options. He also cautions that this is not quite the same as before 2022 — then, more than a hundred thousand Russian troops massing could be clearly seen on the German and Belarusian borders; now there is no such physical preparation. So the most immediate escalation may not be a conventional invasion, but small, ambiguous attacks that can be denied (landing first on warehouses or drones).

23:40 Russia is already probing NATO's limits with drones
At this stage, with no sign of a massed army on the border, Russia still holds a set of low-cost, low-attribution options: a limited strike on a NATO warehouse near Poland or Romania, or a provocation using a captured Ukrainian drone that has been modified, then watching whether NATO splits and whether the US steps in. The guest notes this probing is already underway — an armed drone attacked a Ukrainian aircraft parked at Leipzig airport in Germany, and only a drone malfunction prevented deaths; Russian risk-taking is rising steadily, and the West has so far given no serious response. The senior European officers he speaks with all believe the most dangerous window is the next one to two years, roughly falling in the final phase of Trump's term — the Kremlin will want to act before the US might let go.

27:53 Putin wants Ukraine disarmed, not a ceasefire
Would Putin accept an honorable ceasefire deal? The guest's view is that you only need to look at what is put on the table: Russia has consistently demanded not just territory, but a cap on the size of Ukraine's army, limits on the types of weapons it may hold, and a cutoff of Western military aid to Ukraine. In his words, the goal is to make Ukraine lose the ability to defend itself; not neutral, but emasculated, so that it cannot rise again in the next stage of the war — a year, five years or ten years later. Putin signed Minsk-1 and Minsk-2, and violated both. So the guest quotes the summary of Ukraine's former foreign minister: this war will end in one of only two ways — the end of Ukraine, or the end of the Russian imperial project. Waiting for the other side to change its mind is not an option.

31:08 Street protests can decide the fate of a wartime cabinet
Kyiv's recent personnel earthquake looks on the surface like an anti-corruption storm, but the key mechanism lies elsewhere: elections are frozen in wartime, and the president's legitimacy rests on one ballast stone — street support. Zelensky initially fired Defense Minister Fedorov, the driving force behind drone innovation, because he needed the backing of Commander-in-Chief Syrsky; after Fedorov was dismissed, Kyiv elites took to the streets, and the protests, small as they were, were enough to make the president reverse course — he removed Syrsky, brought in a younger general more popular at the front, and appointed a defense minister with a veteran intelligence background acceptable to all sides. Ukraine's independent anti-corruption bodies can still pursue people in the president's innermost circle, and when Zelensky tried to amend the law to absorb that agency, he backed down within a week under street pressure. When elections are absent, the square equals the ballot box.

38:37 Resistance comes from memory, not heroism
Summing up Ukrainian perseverance as patriotic heroism misses what actually drives them. The guest says that after Russian troops take a Ukrainian town, one of the first things they often do is send bulldozers to tear down monuments to the victims of the 1930s famine — what they want to delete is a memory. Russian state television talks about how to re-educate Ukrainians, to make them forget their language and culture and become Russians. Around World War II the Soviet Union carried out a systematic purge of Ukraine's cultural elite, and in the guest's childhood he did not even know those writers existed, because collective memory had been erased. Ukrainians today are almost all descendants of survivors of that meat grinder, carrying the trauma in their bodies; it is the fear of never again that makes them prefer to die on the battlefield rather than return to that life.

45:59 Half a million veterans blocked the first wave of collapse
On the night of February 23, 2022, most people in Kyiv still did not believe there would be a war; the guest remembers knowing from his experience in Kabul and Baghdad that impossible can flip overnight, but ordinary Ukrainians had no such reference point. What really kept the country from collapsing in the first days was eight years of war in the Donbas: that fighting was far from Kyiv, but it produced roughly 500,000 Ukrainians who had traded blows with the Russian army, and volunteer organizations that evolved into a flexible, aggressive force. The psychological threshold had already been crossed in the Donbas — we know what they look like, we know how to fight them. Because of that experience, the swift collapse Putin expected did not happen, and the West's widespread expectations were wrong too.

item.title: A Child Hitting, Biting or Kicking Isn't Misbehaving — They're Reclaiming Bodily Autonomy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-parentmojo-孩子打咬踢不是坏行为-是在夺回身体自主权/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-parentmojo-孩子打咬踢不是坏行为-是在夺回身体自主权/
item.description: Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. For a three- or four-year-old, hitting, biting and kicking are often the only tool left to shout "I have no say" after adults have taken control of nearly everything their body does — give some choice back, and the behavior shrinks.
item.content:encoded:
Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. For a three- or four-year-old, hitting, biting and kicking are often the only tool left to shout "I have no say" after adults have taken control of nearly everything their body does — give some choice back, and the behavior shrinks.

Most approaches restate "no hitting" and add punishment, never touching the need that precedes the behavior. This episode treats aggression as a need signal, and models the scripts and cases for negotiating with teachers.

4:21 A child hitting is shouting that they can't control their body
Preschool is often the first place a child is controlled in nearly every bodily arrangement by an adult other than a parent: where to sit, how to sit, when to speak and when to move. For the previous three years, they could roughly decide when to run and when to use the toilet. Sitting on a rug for 20 minutes without moving is a real deprivation of autonomy; and a three- or four-year-old has no language to assert "my body is mine to decide," so hitting and kicking become one of the few tools still available. So when the call home comes, don't rush to lecture "hands to yourself" — ask instead: how much say has this child had over their own life until now, and what small piece of it can be handed back?

6:42 Kindergarten readiness is really obedience training
Teachers often say a given preschool has a high share of kindergarten-ready children, and the core definition of that readiness is compliance: sit down when the teacher says sit, even mid-task, even when the body is already overloaded. Parents fear that if the child doesn't comply now, they won't get into a good elementary school, college, a good life. But what the child pays for that definition is learning to suppress the feeling of "what I need right now." Teachers aren't villains either — they too need to feel competent, to keep children safe, to save effort, and even to enjoy some power; many entered education precisely to repair their own childhood wounds, yet only know the power-over model of relationship. Seeing both sides' situations is what opens room to negotiate.

9:24 We grant ourselves regulation and deny it to children
If an adult at a party feels overloaded, they arrive early, leave early, hide in a quiet room, even wear noise-cancelling earplugs — we find that entirely natural. Point the camera at a child, though, and apart from conventions like exam time extensions, we immediately worry that "too much accommodation will spoil them, they'll never survive the real world." The truth is that adults grant themselves far more accommodation than they allow children. The source offers a concrete image: an adult stronger than you unceremoniously carries you out of the quiet room back to the center of the loud party — swap in an adult and you instantly see it as a violation of bodily autonomy; when it happens to a child, we look right past it.

12:11 The repair point is before the behavior, not the behavior itself
Repeating "hitting is not okay" doesn't work, because that isn't the knowledge the child is missing. You need a different set of questions: what happened in the seconds before this bite? What happened earlier in the day? Is there a move or a new baby in the child's life? A sensory-overloaded child who gets jostled in line will melt down, so let them stand at the front, the back, or outside the line; a child who struggles with transitions needs a few minutes' warning. An adult analogy: when your partner snaps at you for no reason at night, it's usually not about that sentence but about the morning's argument, lost sleep, and a pile of stress. If they then tossed off "your attitude needs work," you'd blow up too — yet we routinely do only the latter to children.

15:10 Talking to the teacher: don't assign blame, hear what the "no" protects
Telling a teacher "please change what you do" almost always hits a wall. A safer opening is to drop judgment and reconstruct the facts: don't look for who's responsible, just ask what actually happened; and include family changes, which are context the teacher can't see. Once you know whether the child's trigger is sensory or autonomy, extend empathy to the three things behind the teacher: competence, the child's safety, and the relief of catching a breath. The request must land on a concrete, doable change, like "can the child sit on a ball outside the circle." If the teacher refuses, the keyword isn't the refusal but what need that "no" is still protecting, and finding a different arrangement that meets both sides.

16:07 One nap-time conflict, cleanly taken apart
Jen's daughter Carys, at three, couldn't nap; the teacher wanted her to lie down, and she was bored and frustrated — her need was to play. The teacher had two needs: state rules required offering nap time, and nap time was the teacher's own rest period. The solution they found was to move her mat to a slightly separated corner where she could quietly play with soft toys that wouldn't roll away, and the teacher could see her through the window from the break room. The child kept her right to free play, the teacher kept the rule and her rest, and Jen escaped the no-win cycle of incident reports. This passage shows that "negotiating by need" isn't empty talk: everyone gives a little, but everyone's core need is held.

17:53 Every method comes down to one question
Compress all of the above into a single line: stop asking "how do I make the hitting stop," and ask "what need is this behavior communicating?" Hitting, biting and kicking are only surface signals; the real message may be "I need sensory relief" or "I need some say over my own body." Once the need is correctly named, a path to meeting it can be designed — and it is almost always the adult who changes the environment, because changing how the adult shows up is far easier than changing the child.

item.title: The Thai Flood That Wrecked the Hard Disk Drive Industry: The Biggest Factory Fell, the Number Two Took the Throne
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-asianometry-泰国洪水重创硬盘业-最大的厂跌倒-老二捡了王座/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-asianometry-泰国洪水重创硬盘业-最大的厂跌倒-老二捡了王座/
item.description: One flood in Thailand redrew the hard drive rankings: the largest maker, Western Digital, saw shipments fall 51% quarter over quarter, while Seagate fell only 8% and overtook it to take the top spot.
item.content:encoded:
One flood in Thailand redrew the hard drive rankings: the largest maker, Western Digital, saw shipments fall 51% quarter over quarter, while Seagate fell only 8% and overtook it to take the top spot.

What are the risks of geographic concentration in manufacturing supply chains? This flood is a complete case study — industrial estate siting, zero inventory and a single point of failure all detonating at once.

6:13 Flood walls gave the hard drive makers a false sense of security
The industrial estates were built on river floodplain converted from rice paddies north of Bangkok. For flood protection, developers installed ring levees up to two metres high, secondary wave walls, pumps and drainage systems; the parks quickly grew into small cities with their own housing and shops. But this engineering may have misled everyone. When the real flood season arrived in 2011, seven industrial parks were inundated within two weeks. Research later suspected that precisely this kind of seemingly complete infrastructure created a false confidence — the belief that even if it rained, everything would be fine. In other words, what the manufacturers bought was not safety, but an illusion about risk.

8:24 Reservoir releases were not the culprit; local rainfall was
After the flood, dam managers were blamed for releasing water too late, with criticism centring on favouritism toward farmers and rice-corruption allegations. But the research does not support that blame. A 2023 simulation ran 17 scenarios swapping the release strategies of two dams, and concluded that even with perfect foresight of subsequent rainfall, the flooded area could have been reduced by at most 3.68%. Another 2020 study examined hydrological station data along the Chao Phraya River and found that in one low-lying disaster area, less than 30% of the floodwater came from the river, while 73.7% came from local rainfall. In other words, the water mainly fell directly on the disaster zone; reservoir decisions cannot carry the blame.

9:25 Why Seagate stalled even though it wasn't flooded
Seagate's factories in the north at Korat were basically fine, but production stopped anyway — because seven of its top ten suppliers were underwater. The typical case was Japan's Nidec, which makes spindle motors for hard drives and shut down production outright after two plants flooded. The hard drive supply chain interlocks layer by layer: however safe the assembly line, if the motors don't arrive, the whole line stops. Seagate held its quarterly shipment decline to 8% by quickly qualifying new suppliers, modifying designs to reduce complexity, and negotiating payment terms with suppliers. In the same year, Western Digital's core plant took on water 1.8 metres deep, and its quarterly shipments fell 51%. The difference between the two was not whose building was taller, but whose supply chain could route around the break point faster.

12:34 Zero inventory amplified the flood into a global shortage
Before the flood hit, the hard drive industry had just completed a round of consolidation: Western Digital announced in March 2011 that it would acquire Hitachi's hard drive business, and a month later Seagate announced it would acquire Samsung, barely bringing supply and demand back into balance. Precisely because there was no surplus inventory to draw down, the shock was multiplied. Tom Coughlin estimated that in the fourth quarter of 2011, hard drive demand was about 180 million units while actual production was only 110 million to 120 million; and the flood landed right on the Christmas shopping season. Retail immediately raised spot prices by 20% to 40%; at Taipei's Guanghua Market, a 1TB hard drive went from NT$1,750 to over NT$3,000. Even Intel admitted in December that Q4 revenue would be about $1 billion lower than expected because of the hard drive shortage. A local flood, transmitted through zero inventory, became a global shortage just like that.

15:41 The water receded, but hard drive prices didn't fall for two years
The water receded, but the shortage did not end quickly. Hard drive availability took about nine months to return to pre-disaster levels; retail prices fell back more slowly — hard drive prices on Newegg did not drop back to pre-disaster levels until April 2013. Backblaze did the arithmetic with its own purchasing records: in September 2011 the cost per GB was $0.044, and returning to that level again had to wait until September 2013. Why is it easy to raise prices and hard to cut them? The author lists several interpretations: the ecosystem recovered more slowly than expected, the two giants' 2011 acquisitions brought extra costs, tablets caused PC hard drive demand to fall permanently, and a more cynical guess — after Seagate and Western Digital acquired their second-tier rivals, only three major manufacturers remained in the whole industry, making prices easier to ‘stabilise’, or in his own word: cartelize. As for which one is the truth, he does not conclude.

18:47 The flooded giant chose to stay and keep building walls
Western Digital's post-disaster choice is telling: it did not retreat, it doubled down on defences. WD and the Bang Pa-in estate owner built an 11-kilometre flood wall along the estate, and WD added a 6-metre-high inner wall around its factory; to add redundancy to its supply chain, in December 2011 it announced a new slider fab in Malaysia. A survey of 50 directly affected Japanese companies showed that nearly 80% decided to stay in Thailand. The reasons are not hard to understand: ready-made estates, supporting infrastructure and skilled workers are hard to pack up and take away. Thailand has since suffered several more rounds of major flooding, especially in the 2020s when it happened almost every year; in November of the most recent year it even rained in what was billed as a ‘once in 300 years’ event, but these estates have held out so far. Whether stronger defences will be needed in future can only be tested by the next big flood.

item.title: AI designs viruses that infect bacteria, but only 5% of the time
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-twiv-ai-设计出能感染细菌的病毒-但成功率仅-5/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-twiv-ai-设计出能感染细菌的病毒-但成功率仅-5/
item.description: For the first time, AI designed complete viral genomes from scratch that can infect bacteria; experimental validation puts the success rate at about 5%, nowhere near as omnipotent as the media made it sound.
item.content:encoded:
For the first time, AI designed complete viral genomes from scratch that can infect bacteria; experimental validation puts the success rate at about 5%, nowhere near as omnipotent as the media made it sound.

This episode takes apart the success rate of AI-made viruses, compensatory mutations and biosecurity rhetoric, and also demonstrates how an observational vaccine study can be falsified by an E-value.

12:43 A vaccine switch as a natural control
The trap in "healthy vaccinee bias" is that vaccinated people tend to pay more attention to their own health than unvaccinated people, so comparing the two groups mistakes lifestyle differences for vaccine effects. This study exploits the moment in 2017 when the US shingles vaccine switched wholesale from Zostavax to Shingrix: before the policy switch people received the old vaccine, after it they received the new one, and both groups were people who actively sought vaccination, so in theory the bias is erased. It is still not a randomised trial, however — socioeconomic status, smoking, diet and other unmeasured factors may still be unbalanced between the two groups, so it can only count as a quasi-experiment.

15:47 Weak confounding alone can overturn a vaccine benefit
How strong would unmeasured confounding have to be to overturn an observational conclusion? Measure it with the E-value. The E-value for this vaccine study is only 1.42, almost hugging 1, meaning a confounder that is not even very strong, one associated with both "which vaccine was received" and "cardiovascular outcomes", could explain away the observed risk reduction. An E-value needs to reach 3.4 or even 5 before a conclusion counts as solid; 1.42 is far from robust. The authors themselves admit that a randomised clinical trial is needed to confirm it, and that this observation cannot be treated as evidence.

38:13 AI produces a functional viral genome for the first time
The researchers took the genomic language models EVO1 and EVO2 and had them write phage genomes: first the models read massive public DNA sequence data, then they were fine-tuned on PhiX174 to generate thousands of candidate sequences. Back in the lab for validation, only about 5% of the products could actually infect E. coli — the first time AI has designed a complete genome from scratch that was then proven functional. If the media summarises this as "AI directly created a virus", it misses a key point: the model has only ever seen sequences, with no experimental annotation telling it which base does what, and the 5% hit rate shows how ignorant it still is about how sequence determines function.

44:37 The origin of replication is the model's most conserved memory
The only prompt the model needed was the first 4 to 9 nucleotides of the PhiX174 genome, and the accuracy of the generated results rose significantly. The authors found that this unremarkable stretch is part of the origin of replication, and it was 100% conserved across all the genomes the model generated. It works like a password saying "I am a real virus": the model treats the origin of replication as a core that must be locked down, and only dares to let other positions evolve freely. This also explains why such a short prompt works — what matters is not the prompt's length but whether it hits a functional pressure point.

56:55 AI swaps one gene and adds 58 mutations itself
The design idea behind EVO36 was not to rewrite the whole thing but to swap genes: replace PhiX174's J gene with the shorter J protein from phage G4. When humans performed the same transplant by hand in the past, the product could not infect; but the AI's EVO36 infects normally, because it accumulated 58 additional mutations across the genome. These look like compensatory mutations that exist to re-adapt the foreign J protein to its local environment. Humans might not have thought to touch 58 positions at once, and this is exactly where generative models exceed the capability of single-point editing.

1:00:15 Mixed phages specifically target drug-resistant bacteria
Natural PhiX174 runs into a wall against already resistant bacteria, failing to break through even after five passages; 16 AI-synthesised phages mixed together infected the previously resistant strain within one or two generations. Resistance is not broken by any single phage but by several synthetic phages recombining with each other and accumulating new mutations during replication, finally breaking the barrier through collective action. The result suggests that phage therapy should bet on a cocktail of multiple synthetic phages rather than a single strain.

1:07:29 Don't call AI-made viruses an urgent threat
For that study generating PhiX174, a contemporaneous commentary used the word "urgent" to describe its biosecurity implications. Vincent pushed back on that wording directly on the show: the authors had already shown with reproducible experiments that this kind of research can be done safely, so what is needed is not an alarm bell but the start of building safety frameworks. He also stressed that reconstructing viruses is not science fiction as long as you have enough sequence — which is precisely why frameworks are needed rather than fearmongering.

1:35:53 Not getting vaccinated is often just not knowing
Discussing the unvaccinated population, the article raises an often overlooked mechanism: some people do not get vaccinated not out of religious or ideological opposition, but because they simply do not know they should. Treating vaccine hesitancy uniformly as a "matter of faith" gets the policy response wrong — for this group the key is not debate or persuasion but information outreach so they first learn the vaccine exists.
